nodes.title: The tools
nodes.text: How the SpecSheriff tools carry out the SpecSheriff guidelines, the extensions of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z), and the checks and code generators that a project's own guidelines add (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m, §s-km4x4s26kv7pjze).

decisions.problem: The text of the section "The tools" used the term "the base of the guidelines", which the owner removed, and did not mention the extensions of the guidelines or the checks and code generators that a project's own guidelines add.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("ok") to the agent's proposed wording: "How the SpecSheriff tools carry out the SpecSheriff guidelines, the extensions of the guidelines, and the checks and code generators that a project's own guidelines add."

children.title: Where the files are
children.text:
The SpecSheriff tools find each file of a project at the path given for it below, relative to the root of the repository:

| What is kept | Where |
|---|---|
| The base specification, if the project has not chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm) | `specs/base/` |
| Each domain, if the project has chosen the Domains extension | `specs/<domain>/`, where `<domain>` is the domain's name, which is neither `stack` nor `debt` nor the name of any directory that this table names under `specs/` |
| The contracts section (§s-z6tq6a3btnvvwx7) | `specs/contracts/` |
| The section of the technical appendix (§s-vj7ercem526zd6v) that implements a domain, if the project has chosen the Domains extension | `specs/tech/<domain>.json` |
| The section of the technical appendix that implements the base specification, if the project has not chosen the Domains extension | `specs/tech/base.json` |
| The section of the technical appendix for the stack | `specs/tech/stack.json` |
| The technical debt | `specs/tech/debt.json` |
| The project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) | `specs/_guidelines/project.json` |
| The project's extension of the schema (§s-xm8rz4uupb73gu5) | `specs/_schema/project.schema.json` |
| The approvals of nodes (§s-67vekyup7y8smap) | `specs/_approvals.jsonl` |
| The archive of removed nodes (§s-f2b5zvc565s242f) | every JSON file in `specs/_archive/`, each named after the part of the specification that its nodes were removed from, such as `contracts.json` or `guidelines.json` |
| The bindings file (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4) | `sheriff.bindings.json` |
| The project-wide settings of the SpecSheriff tools, among them the entries that set the specification's approval status (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2) and its `strict` flag (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2), and the extensions of the guidelines that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) | `sheriff.config.json` |
| The map (§s-zu8ne3wq84zchc4) and the human-readable export (§s-ce24ynwabt5yx8h), if the project has chosen the Views extension (§s-qgg6sfawtmwvrbb) | `specs/_viewer/` for the map and `md-version/` for the export, both of which git ignores |
| The documentation | every Markdown file that the repository keeps outside `specs/` |

The files common to every project come with the SpecSheriff tools that a plugin keeps on the machine (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p). The tools find each of these files at the path in the second column of the table below, relative to their own folder, the one that holds their `dist/`. Only the repository where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written keeps these files under `specs/`, each at the path in the third column (§s-6bmnsbskg6en4nf). The SpecSheriff tools recognize that repository only by the environment variable `SPECSHERIFF_GUIDELINES_REPO`, which holds the path to its root. In that repository, the tools read the files at those paths:

| What is kept | Path in the folder of the tools | Path in the repository where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written |
|---|---|---|
| The SpecSheriff guidelines | `guidelines/spec.json` | `specs/_guidelines/spec.json` |
| Each extension of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z) | `guidelines/extensions/<name>.json` | `specs/_guidelines/extensions/<name>.json` |
| The appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8) | `guidelines/tools.json` | `specs/_guidelines/tools.json` |
| The schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines (§s-eferktypcj7njt5): `node.schema.json` for a node, `section-file.schema.json` for a file of a part of the specification, `archive-file.schema.json` for a file of the archive, and `extension.schema.json` for an extension of the schema, whether it is added by an extension of the guidelines or by the project | `guidelines/_schema/` | `specs/_schema/` |
| The schema of `sheriff.config.json`, which sets the default value of the `strict` flag (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2) | `guidelines/_schema/config.schema.json` | `specs/_schema/config.schema.json` |
| The schema of each extension of the guidelines that has one | `guidelines/_schema/extensions/<name>.schema.json` | `specs/_schema/extensions/<name>.schema.json` |
| The meta-schema of a RecordType's `schema` (§s-j4t9vusnsajmqdw) | `guidelines/_schema/extensions/recordtype-meta.schema.json` | `specs/_schema/extensions/recordtype-meta.schema.json` |

`<name>` is the extension's name, which `sheriff.config.json` uses to list the extension once the project has chosen it.
children.reason: The SpecSheriff tools find every file without a setting that says where it is kept, whatever the project and wherever the plugin is installed. A person or an agent who knows where a file is kept in one project finds it in any other. The SpecSheriff tools recognize the repository where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written by an environment variable, so that the settings of every project contain nothing that only that repository needs. The variable holds the path to that repository's root, so that no other repository on the same machine is recognized as that repository.

decisions.problem: The toolset SpecSheriff provides was spelled the toolset, SpecSheriff's toolset and the tools: three names for one thing, the first a general word that does not say whose.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is named the SpecSheriff tools.

decisions.problem: No package installed the command `sheriff` any more: an agent found the SpecSheriff tools through the plugin for Claude Code, and a person's terminal had no command at all.
decisions.ruling: The owner: nothing new is built. In a terminal the command is run from the copy of the tools the plugin keeps in its data directory, whose path is the same on every machine; the agent's skills run it from the tools the plugin carries.

decisions.problem: `pytest-specsheriff`, installed by pip, does not follow the plugin for Claude Code when Claude Code updates it.
decisions.ruling: The owner: nothing is built and no rule says how it is updated. It registers the mark, checks its form and opens the reported name with the sid, while the checks read the sid from the test's source, so an older copy breaks no check; updating it is a person's action, which the practitioner's guide gives.

decisions.problem: By the owner's rule of 2026-10-29, what only the repository the SpecSheriff guidelines are written in does leaves the guidelines for an internal document; this rule says where that repository keeps the guidelines, their schema and its tools, and what it is not read for.
decisions.ruling: The owner: those clauses stay. They say what the SpecSheriff tools do in a repository that writes the guidelines, which every project's copy of the tools carries out; the procedures only that repository runs — a release, the build, running its own plugin — are in its internal document.

decisions.problem: The rule kept every setting of the SpecSheriff tools in sheriff.config.json, which every clone shares, while the settings of the reviewer's runs are each user's to confirm (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u).
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u: the settings of the reviewer's runs are kept in each user's git configuration rather than in sheriff.config.json.

decisions.problem: A project's own schema was refused as a copy, and nothing said where a project's extension, the commands of its checks and generators, the rule putting it live, or its records of history and fixtures are kept.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the extension is `specs/_schema/project.schema.json`; the settings name the commands of a project's checks and generators; the rule putting the specification live and the lists of records of history and fixtures are rules of `project.json`, the tools reading those files from the lists rather than from the settings, so each is said once.

decisions.problem: The rules of how each check is made (§s-4kd2pave7vm4hmd), confirmed by the owner that day, name what this node did not say.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying those rules out: the schema of an extension, the settings naming the code and the tests of each project's own check and generator, the repository's own tools and their tests exempt from tags, no special exemption of the SpecSheriff tools' files from the check of locations.

decisions.problem: The system's code came to include its tests, which carry a sid rather than a tag.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-hheus6f395ynqvc: the repository's configuration, its own tools and their tests are not the system's code because of where they are kept.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: The node named a test's reference to its node a sid, or read a SpecTag as standing only on a symbol, once a test came to carry a SpecTag too.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement in line with the owner's rulings of the same day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: a test names its node by its SpecTag, and the check that binds symbols to their nodes reads only the symbols of code other than tests.

decisions.problem: The node named a node's status checked, the act of agreeing to it a confirmation, the specification's state live, and one owner of a part.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's decision of that day: a node's status is draft or approved, the act is an approval, the specification is approved or a draft, and a part has owners, one or several.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The owner asked what this node is for and for whom, and whether it is auxiliary information rather than a rule. Two of its paragraphs are instructions for a user: how `sheriff` is run in a terminal, and how the plugin for pytest is installed with pip. The practitioner's guide already gives both.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the node stays in the appendix of the tools, since the code of the SpecSheriff tools that finds the files is written from it, and the two instructions are removed from it, since the guide gives them ("ok").

decisions.problem: The proposal gave the paths of the SpecSheriff guidelines and their schema under `specs/` as if every project kept them, kept the entries of the specification's approval status and of its `strict` flag in a file of their own, and listed `specs/_approvals.jsonl`, which T28 is to replace.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines is kept in the plugin's folder, and only the repository where it is written keeps it under `specs/`; the entries of the specification's approval status and of its `strict` flag are kept in `sheriff.config.json`; the row for `specs/_approvals.jsonl` stays until T28.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the revised wording of the node.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to it ("ok").

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the two additions that name the environment variable `SPECSHERIFF_GUIDELINES_REPO`: the sentence before the second table and the two sentences at the end of the reason.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to both ("ok").

decisions.problem: The node cited the Domains extension by its rule on decomposition (s-h6h25ctd3yryudh) rather than by the extension's own section, as specsheriff-rule-reviewer found.
decisions.ruling: The agent made the node cite the section of the extension (s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), a replacement that changes no meaning, and reported it to the owner.

decisions.problem: Whether a draft that only carries out the owner's answers to the questions about the base specification is shown to the owner before it is agreed to.
decisions.ruling: The draft carries out the answer that decision R8 of the page on RecordType and JSON Schema gives to question 4.7 of the questions about the base specification: the meta-schema of a RecordType's `schema` (s-j4t9vusnsajmqdw) is a file of its own beside the schema of the RecordType extension. The reviewer found it ready after the third round of fixes, so it is agreed to on the owner's behalf and reported to the owner in one line.

children.title: Project-wide settings
children.reason: A setting kept in the repository is the same in every clone, so the SpecSheriff tools behave alike for everyone who works on the project.

decisions.problem: The owner asked how the SpecSheriff tools use `"writesSpecSheriffGuidelines": true`, noting that no repository but SpecSheriff's own seems to need it. The tools use the key to tell the repository where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written from a project: only there do they read the guidelines and their schema from `specs/`, judge the approvals of the guidelines' nodes by that repository's own approvals, and accept those files under `specs/` rather than refuse them as copies. `sheriff init` never writes the key, so every project leaves it out.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the key is removed from this node ("ok, remove it"). A setting that only one repository needs is read from an environment variable, since carrying a value that matters to one project into the settings of every other project is an antipattern.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the node without the key `writesSpecSheriffGuidelines`.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to it ("ok").

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 3 of stage 2 of task T25, items 27 to 32 and the owner's ruling of 2026-11-24 on comments and whitespace, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("ok", in answer to "Do you agree to group 3?").

decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group and to option A in both questions ("A.", in answer to "Do you agree to group 7 and to option A in both questions?").

children.title: What the SpecSheriff tools read in the project's own guidelines
children.reason: The SpecSheriff tools need values that only a project's own guidelines set, such as who owns the specification (§s-m42rsngtayk9g3g). A project may give its own rules any titles and arrange those rules as it chooses, so the SpecSheriff tools find each value in the top node of `project.json`, through a link, or through a setting in `sheriff.config.json`.

decisions.problem: On 2026-11-05 the owner ruled, in "The project's own tools in a git hook" (s-n4m5zvh96yb299p), that a project registers its own tools for a hook in a form that the hook can read without the SpecSheriff tools. A list in `project.json` cannot be read without the SpecSheriff tools, yet the agreed rule on the order in which tools and checks run (s-pcnyfp7gev7syax) says that the project's own guidelines list the project's own tools that rewrite files.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the node with that list kept in `project.json` ("ok"). If the SpecSheriff tools cannot run, a git hook runs all the project's own tools in the bytewise order of their names, as it does now; no check required by the SpecSheriff guidelines runs in that case anyway.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to group 4 of stage 2 of task T25, items 33 to 40, row 10.1.37a and the proposals on rule 10.12, row 10.1.41 and `new:tools-1-project`, shown on one page with each node in full.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group ("A", in answer to "Do you choose A? If so, and you have no remarks on the nodes, the same answer agrees to the whole of group 4.").

children.title: The commands
children.text: What each command of the SpecSheriff tools does, and which node describes it.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the section "The commands", which states its purpose, and to the order of the eleven nodes under it.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the section and to the order ("ok").

children.title: The commands that `sheriff` accepts
children.reason: A reader who knows what has to be done, or the name of a command, finds here the command for the task and the nodes that describe everything the command does.

decisions.problem: The types and runtime checks generated from the data record nodes had no command.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a command of their own generates them.

decisions.problem: The reindex read every file through a parser that keeps the last of two values under one key and drops the first, and wrote back what it read: a ruling written under a second decisions key of a node's metadata hid two earlier rulings on the same rule from every tool, and the next reindex would have deleted them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reindex merges the two values, names each merge, and refuses two it cannot merge, naming both.

decisions.problem: A command reported a citation as a candidate for a link nobody typed, and the citation check, which a commit runs, was named by no rule.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's rulings on citations (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz, §s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws): the command that reported candidates for citation is removed, and the citation check is listed among the commands.

decisions.problem: The commands were one repository's package scripts.
decisions.ruling: The owner: they are the commands of the SpecSheriff tools, described in the appendix of the tools.

decisions.problem: The first sentence gave `sheriff binding` every check between the specification and the code, though the table of how each check is made gives some of them to other commands.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the sentence names the commands that check and leaves to that table which check each makes, so that it is said in one place.

decisions.problem: The rule on sheriff types said neither which files it writes nor what it refuses, and the tool rewrote every listed file at every run, though it now runs after every edit an agent makes and at every commit; the rule read as one block of text, and named the map without saying what it is.
decisions.ruling: The owner: sheriff types writes a file only where its content changes, names each file it writes, and writes nothing where anything is refused; the checks are implemented as the table describes them; the map is named as the mindmap of the specification's structure; each command stands in a paragraph of its own, sheriff init before sheriff reindex.

decisions.problem: sheriff types wrote the types and runtime checks from data record nodes whether or not they were checked.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j: code generated from the nodes waits until every node it is generated from is approved. No commit changes it in the meantime, and its lag is reported.

decisions.problem: A project's own checks and generators had no way to read the model, the values gathered beside a field had nothing writing them, and nothing gave the model to a program outside the tools.
decisions.ruling: The owner: `sheriff model` prints the model as JSON, handed to a project's check or generator on its standard input; `sheriff types` writes the files a project's generator prints, on the terms of the types; the reindex writes the gathered values; which command runs a project's checks is said in the table of how each check is made.

decisions.problem: No command listed the work put off on the nodes, kept in their todos.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's rule on work put off (§s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh): `sheriff todos` lists every item, the newest first, each with its node.

decisions.problem: The node named a kind of node "data record" and a node's place "address" or "id".
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.problem: The owner renamed a node's id to location, its rationale to reason and the kind record to RecordType, while every project's files and confirmations hold the old names.
decisions.ruling: A technical consequence in the owner's name: the reindex renames them in every file once.

decisions.problem: Earlier releases wrote an empty own list for a field whose values the domains add, while a field now names its one source.
decisions.ruling: A technical consequence of the owner's rule on one source for a field's values, in the owner's name: the reindex gives such a field the values the domains add as its source.

decisions.problem: `sheriff types` wrote no file while any RecordType, any node a project's generator writes from or any rule listing a generator was unchecked, while the check of generated copies held each kind of copy to its own nodes: a generator's file confirmed while an unrelated RecordType waited could be neither written nor committed.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the owner's rule that what is generated waits for the nodes it is generated from (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j): each file waits only for its own nodes, here and in the check of generated copies (§s-dbk2vyeg8z5jxna).

decisions.problem: Tests written for an earlier release named their node by a bare sid, which a release reading the SpecTag would refuse at the next commit once the plugin updated itself.
decisions.ruling: Carrying out the reason of this rule: the release rewrites the earlier form itself, and the project rewrites nothing by hand.

decisions.problem: The reindex emptied a node's status and confirmed sections as rules, and a release left earlier statuses, owners and confirmations in the files.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's rulings on §s-5ah25f6gy99panq, §s-9kfdycuq34beqvs and §s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2: the reindex makes a node a draft, derives the approval status of sections and headers, adds the rule that represents the specification's approval status where it is missing, and rewrites what earlier releases wrote.

decisions.problem: The owner settled the vocabulary of the method: the kind values equal the names, so the kind rule is TextRule, the kind record type RecordType and the kind naming a domain's header header.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out that decision: the reindex renames the earlier kind values in every file, where a field's values are the sids of a kind's nodes, and where the project's extension adds fields to a kind.

decisions.problem: The node was written before the rules of one thought to a sentence (s-juucyammgq4shq8) and of what is applied together (s-6j8ystpj2yzcchq), and before the names of the method were settled.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying out those rules and the names the owner settled on 2026-11-07: the wording rewritten, its meaning unchanged.

decisions.problem: The names of four commands did not say what the commands do: `sheriff message` checks a commit's message against the code that the commit changes, `sheriff model` prints the specification as JSON data, `sheriff export` writes the specification in Markdown, and `sheriff render` writes the map of the specification. The owner proposed `sheriff commit`, `sheriff json_schema`, `sheriff markdown` and `sheriff map`. The agent proposed `sheriff json`, since the command prints the specification and not its JSON Schema, and `sheriff commit-message`, since `sheriff commit` could be read as a command that makes a commit.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the commands are renamed `sheriff commit-message`, `sheriff json`, `sheriff markdown` and `sheriff map` ("ok").

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the node, which lists each command with what it is for, under the new names of four commands.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the node ("ok").

decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group and to option A in both questions ("A.", in answer to "Do you agree to group 7 and to option A in both questions?").

children.title: What `sheriff reindex` changes in what an earlier release wrote
children.reason: Each file and each test of a project follows the form used by the release of the SpecSheriff tools that last wrote or read it. A release that writes or reads them in a different form rewrites them, so that nobody has to rewrite a project by hand and no approval is lost because of a rename.
examples: In a project that an earlier release set up, the only rule of `project.json` is an approved rule that refines the rule on the specification's approval status. `sheriff reindex` replaces that rule with an entry that approves the specification and, in the same run, adds the draft rule on when the tests run. The most likely mistake is to add that draft rule again in a later run, after the project has deleted it.

decisions.problem: Four cases of an earlier RecordType have no exact counterpart in JSON Schema: a field required "where it holds a value", a field of the type `variant`, a field whose values came from the source `domains`, which the owner removed, and a field whose own list of values is empty, which an earlier release read as that source.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("ok") to the agent's proposal: a field required "where it holds a value" becomes an optional property, since JSON Schema checks the value of an optional property where it is present. `sheriff reindex` leaves a RecordType that holds any of the other three in its earlier form and names it and each such field, for its author to rewrite, since a guessed mapping could change the meaning unnoticed.

children.title: Keys written more than once
children.reason: `sheriff reindex` rewrites the files written by hand in full, so it keeps everything they hold. Each of two values written under one key expresses somebody's intent. They are kept together where both can be kept. They are refused where keeping one would drop the other, since nothing says which was meant. Every merge is named, because one of the two values may have been written to replace the other.
examples: A node holds `"refs": [A]` and, further down, `"refs": [B, A]`: `sheriff reindex` writes `"refs": [A, B]` and names `refs` with the line numbers of both values. `sheriff reindex` refuses a node that holds `"title": "X"` and `"title": "Y"`, and writes no file.

decisions.problem: Whether the merge of keys written twice also covers the project's extension of the schema, `specs/_schema/project.schema.json`, which is written by hand and which row 10.1.1 covers.

children.title: What `sheriff types` generates
children.text:
`sheriff types` generates, from the last approved wording of each node (§s-qyjw8xez6t6adc3), the parts of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) that are derived from the nodes:
- the types and the RuntimeChecks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9) generated from the RecordTypes (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3), in the files that the technical appendix lists for them (§s-pvzms7d8kxb8dk2);
- the files that each of the project's own code generators prints (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze, §s-y5yk7eu6h4zrjpr).

The last approved wording of a node is the wording whose fingerprint the node's last approval records (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb). `sheriff types` takes that wording from the files of the specification where they hold it. Otherwise it takes the wording from the latest commit on the current branch whose files hold it, and reads that wording in the form into which `sheriff reindex` would rewrite it (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv).

Where neither holds that wording, `sheriff types` names the node and takes the latest wording that an approval of the node records and that the files or the current branch hold. Where there is none, it treats the node as never approved.

`sheriff types` treats only a RecordType as relying on other nodes. A RecordType relies on each of the following RecordTypes, directly or through other RecordTypes:
- each RecordType that it refines;
- each RecordType that one of its fields refers to.

`sheriff types` takes the `refines` links of a RecordType from the commit that added the RecordType's last approval to `specs/_approvals.jsonl`, and from the files of the specification until that commit is made.

`sheriff types` names by its sid each node that it leaves out because that node relies on a node that has never been approved (§s-f8fmudceuyaj942).

`sheriff types` generates the types and RuntimeChecks from the gathered values written beside a field (§s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh) as the files of the specification hold them when it runs, even when a RecordType's approved wording is taken from a commit.

`sheriff types` writes a file only where the file is missing or holds, line endings aside, content other than what it generates. It names each file that it writes.

If any of the following is true, `sheriff types` names each refusal and writes no file:
- the check of generated copies against the nodes refuses anything that `sheriff types` would write (§s-dbk2vyeg8z5jxna);
- `sheriff types` refuses a project's generator (§s-y5yk7eu6h4zrjpr).
children.reason: `sheriff types` regenerates the code that comes from the nodes after every edit and at every commit (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j). Each run therefore changes only what a change in the approved wordings affects, and leaves that code either wholly regenerated or untouched.

decisions.problem: The values gathered beside a field come, for example, from domain headers, which nobody approves, so a RecordType that waited for their approval would never be generated. A RecordType's `refines` links are not part of its approved wording, so a link added after the approval would change the generated type without an approval.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("ok") to the agent's proposals: the types and RuntimeChecks are generated from the gathered values as the files of the specification hold them when `sheriff types` runs; `sheriff types` takes a RecordType's `refines` links from the commit that added the RecordType's last approval to `specs/_approvals.jsonl`, and from the files while that commit has yet to be made. The node had been shown in full with both paragraphs, and the owner's answer agreed to the node as well.

children.title: How a project's own code generator is run
children.reason: A project's own generator is a program that the SpecSheriff tools did not write, yet what it prints becomes the system's code. `sheriff types` therefore decides what the generator reads and which part of its output is written, so that the generated code implements only what the owners have approved (§s-qyjw8xez6t6adc3).

decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("ok") to the agent's proposals: `sheriff types` refuses a generator that prints a path outside the system's code, and one that prints a file whose `sids` name a node outside the model that the generator is handed. The node had been shown in full with both refusals, and the owner's answer agreed to the node as well.

children.title: The model of the specification
children.text:
`sheriff json` prints, as JSON, the model of the specification of the repository in which it runs.

The model holds each node of the files that the repository keeps. It also holds each node of the SpecSheriff guidelines, of the chosen extensions (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) and of the appendix of the tools, where the project takes them from the plugin. It also holds each node that is in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6).

It gives each node in the form in which its file holds it, without the nodes under it, together with:
- the part of the specification and the file that the node is in;
- the node above it;
- the owners named by the nearest section or domain header above it that names owners (§s-6sk8uet75dmq5qz).

The model also holds the specification's approval status (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2) and its `strict` flag (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2).
children.reason: Given the model instead of reading the files itself, a project's check or code generator finds nodes by their location, finds owners and follows links as the SpecSheriff tools do, in whatever programming language the project writes that check or generator. The approval status and the `strict` flag are in the model because they affect what a project's check requires.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the node on the model of the specification that `sheriff json` prints.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the node ("ok").

children.title: The list of todos
children.text:
`sheriff todos` prints as plain text every item of `meta.todos` (§s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh) of the nodes in the files that the repository keeps.

The items are listed newest first. Items of the same day are sorted by the path of their file, compared in code-point order, and then in the order in which their nodes appear in that file. Each item is printed with its date, its author, the work to be done, and the sid, the location and the title of its node.
children.reason: A todo is kept on the node it concerns (§s-t28j22vbdmmeqnh), so it can be found where that node is. Listed together, the todos show all the deferred work in one place, newest first.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the node on the list of the todos that `sheriff todos` prints.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the node ("ok").

children.title: The guidelines that a project follows, printed in one place
children.text:
`sheriff guide` prints the guidelines that the project follows, each node with its links and without its metadata (§s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7):
- the SpecSheriff guidelines;
- each extension of the guidelines that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g);
- the project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu).

For each of the other extensions that the plugin delivers, `sheriff guide` prints the extension's name and what the extension is for.

After the guidelines, `sheriff guide` prints the appendix of the tools, under a heading that says the appendix is not part of the guidelines (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8).

`sheriff guide` also prints how many nodes each part of the specification holds and how many of those nodes are approved. It counts them each time it runs. It prints whether the specification is approved (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2) and whether the specification's `strict` flag is on (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2).
children.reason: An agent reads the guidelines before it works on the specification. Printed by one command, they are exactly the rules that the project follows, whatever release of the SpecSheriff tools it uses and whichever extensions it has chosen. The appendix of the tools comes after them because it holds what an agent needs to apply them with the SpecSheriff tools, such as the syntax of the SpecTag.

decisions.problem: The plan for splitting "The commands", which the owner agreed to on 2026-11-21, left the appendix of the tools out of what `sheriff guide` prints. The syntax of the SpecTag, the commands and the hooks are described only in that appendix, and the skill `spec` tells an agent to read what `sheriff guide` prints before anything else.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed ("ok") to the agent's proposal: `sheriff guide` prints the appendix of the tools after the guidelines, under a heading that says the appendix is not part of them. The node had been shown in full with that paragraph, and the owner's answer agreed to the node as well.

children.title: The settings that only an owner of the specification changes
children.text:
`sheriff settings` shows and changes the settings that only an owner of the specification changes: the specification's approval status (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2), its `strict` flag (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2), and the extensions of the guidelines that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g).

Run in a terminal with no arguments, `sheriff settings` shows the settings that only an owner changes, and every extension that the plugin delivers. It then lets the person who runs it change each of them. Run with no terminal attached and with no arguments, it prints them.

Run with one of the following sets of arguments, `sheriff settings` makes that one change:
- `status approved` or `status draft`, for the specification's approval status;
- `strict on` or `strict off`, for the `strict` flag;
- `extension <name> on` or `extension <name> off`, for the choice of an extension.

`sheriff settings` records each change as an entry in `sheriff.config.json` that names the person who made the change, by the email address set in git's configuration. It records a change only when that person is an owner of the specification (§s-6sk8uet75dmq5qz), and refuses it otherwise.

`sheriff settings` records or refuses each change as required by the rules on the approval status, on the `strict` flag and on withdrawing an extension (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2, §s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2, §s-j8y62pa9hzz6nwx). Where those rules require the owner to confirm an approval and no terminal is attached, the owner confirms it by adding `--confirm` to `status approved`, personally or through an agent working for that owner.

`sheriff settings` records the choice of an extension only where the plugin delivers that extension (§s-j5qmmdq4m26mdvw).

A refusal caused by the `strict` flag names, for each check that would refuse, the command that lists what that check finds:
- `sheriff untagged`, for the check for code that no SpecTag binds (§s-weuyx98r7c923ab);
- `sheriff validate --strict`, for a project's own checks: it runs the project's own checks as if the specification were approved and its `strict` flag were on (§s-7pk89t8z6wymmj9).
children.reason: An agent may record a change to the specification's approval status, its `strict` flag or its chosen extensions only through a procedure (§s-83ev4wwesbwnhnp). `sheriff settings` is that procedure, for an owner at a terminal and for an agent working for that owner alike.
examples: The agent runs `sheriff settings status approved`. The checks find two symbols without a SpecTag, and the command prints them and records nothing. The owner agrees, and the agent runs `sheriff settings status approved --confirm`. But not: the first run records the approval.

decisions.problem: Whether the owner agrees to the node on `sheriff settings`, with its arguments, `--confirm`, its example and `sheriff validate --strict`.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the node ("ok").

children.title: The entries of the settings that only an owner changes
children.text:
`sheriff.config.json` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u) keeps the entries of each setting that only an owner of the specification changes (§s-chsfpkgpmfk4fft) in a list of its own, under its own key:
- `approvalStatus`, for the specification's approval status (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2): each entry holds `status`, whose value is `approved` or `draft`, and `by`;
- `strict`, for the specification's `strict` flag (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2): each entry holds `on`, whose value is `true` or `false`, and `by`;
- `extensions`, for the extensions of the guidelines that the project has chosen (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g): each entry holds `name`, whose value is the name of an extension (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u), `chosen`, whose value is `true` or `false`, and `by`.

An entry's `by` holds the email address of the owner who made the change that the entry records. An entry holds only the keys given above for its list.

`sheriff settings` (§s-chsfpkgpmfk4fft) appends each entry to the end of its list. In a commit, each list begins with the entries that the commit's parent holds in that list (§s-j9r8z4xdrfkfs47). So the last entry of a list is the latest.

The specification's approval status and its `strict` flag each have the value that the last entry of that setting's list sets. The project has chosen exactly those extensions for which the last entry that names the extension sets `chosen` to `true`.

Where `sheriff.config.json` holds no entry for the approval status, no owner has approved the specification. The specification is then a draft (§s-9g7jj8z4yf9kq93). Where `sheriff.config.json` holds no entry for the `strict` flag, the flag has the value that the schema of `sheriff.config.json` gives as the `default` of an entry's `on` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u).

`sheriff settings` records an entry only where the entry changes the value of its setting.
children.reason: The entries record every change that an owner has made to the settings that only an owner of the specification changes, each with the email address of the owner who made it, but only the last entry of each list sets the value of its setting. `sheriff reindex` writes an entry in place of the rule through which an owner approved the specification in an earlier release (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv). Since no entry holds anything that depends on when it is written, the check on the entries (§s-j9r8z4xdrfkfs47) never mistakes the entry that `sheriff reindex` writes for an entry that was changed.
examples: `approvalStatus` holds `{"status": "approved", "by": "a@example.com"}` followed by `{"status": "draft", "by": "b@example.com"}`. The specification is a draft, since the last entry makes it a draft again. The most likely mistake is to treat the specification as approved because one of the entries approves it.

children.title: Approving the specification
children.reason: The checks at a commit judge only what the commit contains, so they never show everything that the specification and the code still lack (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2). The checks before an approval judge the whole specification and all of the code as one commit, so they show the owner everything that is still missing before the owner approves the specification.
examples: The specification is a draft, and its `strict` flag is off. An approved rule R has neither code nor a test, and an old function has no SpecTag. The agent runs `sheriff settings status approved` with no terminal attached. `sheriff settings` names R, saying that R lacks code and a test, names the function, and records nothing. The owner agrees to the approval, and the agent runs the command again with `--confirm`. The most likely mistake is to treat R's approval as one that was in force before the single commit that the checks assume. R is then not among the rules that the assumed commit includes, and the owner never sees what R lacks.

children.title: Turning the `strict` flag on
children.text:
`sheriff settings` (§s-chsfpkgpmfk4fft) refuses to turn the `strict` flag on (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2) where a check that the flag makes stricter would refuse a commit or a push that changes nothing. It runs these checks on the files in the working tree, as if the specification were approved and the flag were on. The refusal names, for each check that would refuse, the command that lists what that check finds. Where no such check would refuse, `sheriff settings` records the entry that turns the flag on (§s-d3nkw9b6mn98vuw).

The checks that the `strict` flag makes stricter, the cases in which each would refuse a commit or a push that changes nothing, and the command that the refusal to turn the flag on names for each are the following:
- the check for code and tests outside the commit (§s-3xx2eukc8gtd2tx) that no SpecTag (§s-8xw4mgvpexyvw5q) binds: it would refuse where `sheriff untagged` (§s-weuyx98r7c923ab) would list anything, and the refusal to turn the flag on names `sheriff untagged`;
- each of the project's own checks (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m), any of which a rule of the project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) may make stricter (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2): such a check would refuse where `sheriff validate --strict` would refuse because of that check (§s-7pk89t8z6wymmj9), and the refusal to turn the flag on names `sheriff validate --strict`.

`sheriff settings` also refuses to turn the `strict` flag on while the files of the specification fail the check for a key written more than once (§s-7zqsstgnuc772ba) or the validation against their schema (§s-xzcw3hv4hmxz7h7). The refusal names `sheriff validate`, which lists what those checks find.
children.reason: The flag lets the owners make the checks stricter by an act of their own without stopping all work when they do (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2). Turned on while a check that it makes stricter would refuse a commit that changes nothing, the flag would make every commit fail, or keep the specification from being approved, until that check passed.
examples: The specification is a draft, and two functions in an old file have no SpecTag. An owner runs `sheriff settings strict on`. `sheriff settings` refuses to turn the flag on and names `sheriff untagged`, which lists those functions. The most likely mistake is to turn the flag on because the specification is a draft. `sheriff settings` then refuses to approve the specification until each of the two functions has a SpecTag.

children.title: The list of code that no SpecTag binds
children.text:
`sheriff untagged` lists, by file and symbol, the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) that no SpecTag (§s-8xw4mgvpexyvw5q) binds (§s-3xx2eukc8gtd2tx), including the tests. The check for such code names this command in its warning and in its refusal (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn).

`sheriff untagged` names the code outside every symbol of a file, which the SpecSheriff tools treat as one more symbol (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2), by the file's name alone.
children.reason: In one warning, the check covers all the code that no SpecTag binds, so that the warning does not bury the other findings (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn). `sheriff untagged` lists that code symbol by symbol for whoever has to bind each symbol to the rules it implements.
examples: An old function carries the SpecTag `@spec s-…`, which names a section, and no other SpecTag. `sheriff untagged` lists the function with its file, since that SpecTag binds nothing. The most likely mistake is to list only code that carries no SpecTag at all, so that the function is missing from the list that the warning points to.

children.title: Setting a repository up and taking SpecSheriff out of it
children.reason: Adopting the method and removing it each take one command, so that nobody has to know every file and setting that the SpecSheriff tools need. What `sheriff init` writes reaches every clone through git, so the checks run the same way for everyone who works on the project (§s-epaw9sgyaajzn8g). Each command changes only what serves the SpecSheriff tools, and leaves the rest of the repository to the project.
examples: Someone runs `sheriff init` in a project on Windows. Git on Windows does not read the executable mode from a file, so `sheriff init` stages each hook that it wrote with the mode 100755 and names it. The most likely mistake is to make the hooks executable on disk only: git on Windows does not record that mode, so a clone on Linux or macOS runs none of the hooks.

Two branches each approve a node, and each appends a line to `specs/_approvals.jsonl`. Because `sheriff init` configured git to merge that file by union, the merge keeps both lines and puts the line from the branch being merged after the line from the current branch. Without the union merge, git would report a conflict in that file. The most likely mistake is to resolve that conflict by keeping the lines of one branch, which loses the approval made on the other branch.

The owner runs `sheriff init` in a new repository. `project.json` then holds a section that names the owner and holds, as a draft, the rule on when the tests run. So the first commit passes the check that every section contains a rule (§s-exxuckgakfxkycp). The most likely mistake is to write the section without a rule, so that the check refuses the first commit.

decisions.problem: sheriff init made the hooks executable with chmod, which git on Windows does not see, so a project set up there committed them as not executable, and a clone on Linux or macOS ran none of its checks, git skipping each hook with a hint: the worked example's recorded run went through there unrefused.
decisions.ruling: The owner: sheriff init stages each hook it holds with the executable mode where git's index does not already hold it so, naming each, and nothing else, and where it cannot stage a hook says how to.

decisions.problem: Nothing set a new project up live or as a draft.
decisions.ruling: The owner: `sheriff init` writes the rule putting the specification live, unchecked, where the repository keeps no file in a language the tools read for tags, read from the files since the settings it writes name no code yet.

decisions.problem: A hook finding no SpecSheriff tools turned the git hooks off, and taking the method up or out moved where git looks for hooks, either of which stops the project's own tools in silence.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-pcnyfp7gev7syax: `sheriff init` names each hook the repository ran before from elsewhere, and `sheriff remove` each folder of the project's own tools it leaves.

decisions.problem: The node called the mark binding a symbol to the node it implements a tag.
decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decision of that day: a tag is called SpecTag.

decisions.problem: `sheriff init` wrote the rule putting the specification live only where the repository held no code, and unchecked, so the first commit was refused until its owner confirmed it.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2: the rule is written in every project, as a draft; the specification of a project without code stays a draft until its owners approve the rule.

decisions.problem: Two branches that each appended a line to the approvals conflicted where they were merged, while the reason of §s-v4qus7raqnwzneb held that they merge without one.
decisions.ruling: The owner: `sheriff init` has git merge the approvals by union, by a line of `.gitattributes`, and `sheriff remove` takes the line out.

children.title: Building the map
children.reason: A person opens the map wherever the repository is, often without network access. On the map, the person sees the approval status of every node at a glance, at whatever size the map is drawn. The map is drawn from the nodes alone, with nothing stored between the nodes and the page, so it never shows a structure that the nodes no longer have (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).
examples: A project that has chosen the Views and Domains extensions lists the levels `core` and `services`. The domain `requests` is at the level `core`, and the domains `accounts` and `billing` are at the level `services`, and `billing` uses `accounts`. The branch `Base specification` holds the top-level node of the contracts section first, and then the headers of `requests`, `accounts` and `billing`, in that order, each with the sections of its domain under it. A `TableRule` in a section of `requests` holds the nodes in its cells under it, each labelled with its location. The most likely mistake is to take the domains in the alphabetical order of their names, which puts `accounts` before `requests`, although `requests` is in a higher row of the diagram of the domains.

children.title: Drawing the diagram of the domains

examples: The domains `a`, `b`, `c`, `d` and `e` are at the same level. `a` uses `b` and `c`, `c` uses `d`, and `e` has no link to any domain of the row. The row is `e`, `b`, `d`, `c`, `a`: `e` comes first, and `a` comes after `b` and after `c`, which comes after `d`. The most likely mistake is to place `a` right after `b`, the first domain that it uses, which puts `a` to the left of `c`, which it also uses.

children.title: How a node is written in Markdown
children.reason: Every command that writes a node for a reader writes it in the same form, so a reader who knows that form from one command can read the output of any other. In that form, a reader sees everything that the node's file holds for the node, and where each of its links leads, without opening the file (§s-ce24ynwabt5yx8h).
examples: The main table of checks (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh) is a `TableRule` whose column “What is checked” holds a node in each row and whose column “On failure” holds text. `sheriff show` prints the node of one of its rows under a heading that holds the node's location. Along with the node, `sheriff show` prints the heading “What is checked” of the node's column, the heading of its group, such as “The specification alone”, and the text of its row's cell under “On failure”, such as “refused”. The most likely mistake is to print the node without the text of its row, so its reader does not see what a failure of the check costs.

children.title: Writing the human-readable export
children.text:
`sheriff markdown` writes the human-readable export (§s-ce24ynwabt5yx8h) only where the project has chosen the Views extension (§s-qgg6sfawtmwvrbb, §s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g). In any other project, it refuses to run. The refusal names the Views extension.

`sheriff markdown` writes the export into `md-version/` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u) as follows:
- it first removes everything in that folder;
- it then writes two kinds of file there: a `.gitignore` file that holds `*`, and the Markdown files.

That `.gitignore` file makes git ignore the folder's contents whatever the repository's own ignore files say.

`sheriff markdown` writes one Markdown file for each file of the specification whose nodes the model of the specification holds (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx). These include the files of the SpecSheriff guidelines, of the chosen extensions and of the appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8) that the project takes from the plugin (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab, §s-zefk589ykh37b8u).

The path of each Markdown file is the path of its source file under `specs/`, placed under `md-version/`, with `.md` in place of `.json`. For a file that the project takes from the plugin, its path under `specs/` is the one at which the repository where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written keeps that file (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u).

Each Markdown file holds the top-level nodes of its source file, in the order in which the file holds them. Each of them is written as a node is written in Markdown (§s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7), followed by all the nodes under it.
children.reason: In the export, a person reads the project's whole specification, including the guidelines that the project takes from the plugin. The export is written anew from the nodes on every run and kept out of git, so it never becomes a second copy of the specification that a commit could change (§s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j).
examples: A project that has chosen the Views and Domains extensions keeps `specs/_guidelines/project.json`, `specs/contracts/terms.json` and `specs/requests/intake.json`, and takes the SpecSheriff guidelines, the files of those extensions and the appendix of the tools from the plugin. `sheriff markdown` writes `md-version/_guidelines/project.md`, `md-version/contracts/terms.md`, `md-version/requests/intake.md`, `md-version/_guidelines/spec.md`, `md-version/_guidelines/extensions/domains.md`, `md-version/_guidelines/extensions/views.md` and `md-version/_guidelines/tools.md`. The most likely mistake is to write only the files that the repository keeps, which leaves the guidelines that the project follows out of the export.

children.title: Printing one node
children.text:
`sheriff show` prints one node to its standard output, written as a node is written in Markdown (§s-k4nqjr96ux7a5m7), without the nodes under it. The command's argument is that node's sid (§s-9spq78kdwsxr759) or location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx).

`sheriff show` looks for the node among the nodes that the model of the specification holds (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx), including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6). Where none of them has that sid or that location, `sheriff show` refuses the argument and names it. `sheriff show` refuses to run without an argument.
children.reason: A node is read on its own (§s-x4zcbk5ekebd9ua). `sheriff show` gives a person or an agent everything that a node's file holds for that node, and where each of its links leads, so that they need not open the files of the specification.
examples: `sheriff show _guidelines/spec/8.5` prints the rule that is at that location in the same form in which `sheriff show` prints it when it is given that rule's sid. The most likely mistake is to look the argument up among the sids alone, so a location is refused.

children.title: The hooks
children.reason: A check reads the commit being made, because judging anything else would pass or refuse what is not being committed. The hooks that the repository keeps and those that the plugin for Claude Code declares run each check at the moment set for it in every clone, whoever makes the change (§s-epaw9sgyaajzn8g).
examples: A developer stages a change to rule R and leaves a second change to R unstaged. On the commit, `sheriff validate` reads R as it is staged. The most likely mistake is to run the checks on the working tree, so that they judge the second change, which the commit does not hold.

decisions.problem: The citation check was run by no hook, so citations it refused reached the main branch through commits every hook had passed, and nothing checked that a citation in a node had a link.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's rulings on citations (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz, §s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm, §s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws): the pre-commit hook runs the citation check, and the check of the specification refuses a citation with no link.

decisions.problem: An automated security review found that the plugin's session start turns on whatever hooks `.githooks/` holds in a repository whose root holds `sheriff.config.json`, so a repository someone opens could have git run code it brought, which git never does for a clone until its user turns its hooks on.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule stands, and nothing is built against it. The consent that counts is the trust a user gives a folder in Claude Code, before which a plugin the project declares does not load; a repository taking the method runs its own code at every push anyway, since the pre-push hook runs its tests; and the case left open needs together the plugin installed by the user rather than declared by the project, Claude Code run without its dialog of trust, and a clone nobody looked at.

decisions.problem: The todo on this rule asks for post-merge and post-checkout hooks writing the export and the map, which follow a change that reaches the working tree through git only at the next edit an agent makes or the next commit.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it waits past the first release, 0.1.0, and the todo stays. The export and the map are views kept in the working tree, which git does not keep and no check reads, and they lag only until the next edit or commit.

decisions.problem: Nothing ran sheriff types, so after a change to a data record node the generated types and runtime checks stayed behind the nodes until somebody remembered to run it, while the base requires what is generated from the nodes to be regenerated after every change to them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the agent's hooks run sheriff types after every edit, before the checks; the pre-commit hook runs it last, after the checks and whatever they found, on what is staged, its refusal stopping the commit and each file it writes copied into the working tree for the author to stage, nothing staged by the hook.

decisions.problem: The pre-push hook ran the tests over the working tree, its uncommitted changes and files never added included, while every check reads the commit being made and never what it does not hold.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the push is refused while the working tree differs from what it sends, files it ignores left aside, rather than the hook setting such changes aside itself; then the tests run in the working tree.

decisions.problem: The pre-commit hook stopped a commit where the export or the map could not be written from the working tree, as from a specification file broken there and not staged, though the commit holds neither.
decisions.ruling: Following §s-jau82aq9juv9zzh: a failure to write the export or the map at a commit is reported and stops nothing.

decisions.problem: The reason had the types regenerated after every change to the nodes, while they now wait until every node they are generated from is checked.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-kh8qcd5kxgh9z3j: code generated from the nodes waits until every node it is generated from is approved. No commit changes it in the meantime, and its lag is reported.

decisions.problem: A repository whose hooks git's index held without the executable mode, as one set up on Windows did, ran none of its checks in a clone on Linux or macOS, git skipping each hook with a hint, and nothing told its user so.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the session start names each git hook git's index holds without the executable mode and, where files keep that bit, each whose file lacks it, says how to make it executable on every system, and changes neither a file's mode nor the index.

decisions.problem: The reviewer runs at the settings each user confirms (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u), and nothing asked a user for them or wrote them where the git hooks read them.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the settings of the reviewer are a decision taken once, when the plugin is installed, not a question at each session; Claude Code asks for them as the plugin's options, which the session start of the plugin for Claude Code writes into the git configuration in any repository and wherever they differ, so that a change made in /config reaches the reviewer; Codex, which asks nothing at installation, has the agent ask at the first session in a repository taking the method, or spec-init where it runs first; the question is put once on each machine, and after it only the notice at each review reminds the user.

decisions.problem: The after-edit hook ran every step after every shell command, a read-only one included, which took most of a minute on a large repository; it missed PowerShell; and the agent was never told a node its edit had left unchecked. The pre-push hook ran the tests of the system's code alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the checks run after an edit only where the last commit or the working tree changed since they last ran, the regeneration only where `specs/` or the settings changed; PowerShell is read as Bash is; each status emptied is reported; the tests of a project's own checks and generators run before a push with the system's.

decisions.problem: The rules of how each check is made (§s-4kd2pave7vm4hmd), confirmed by the owner that day, name what this node did not say.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying those rules out: the regeneration after an edit also runs where the code of a project's own generator differs.

decisions.problem: The tools the method was extracted with ran the review even where the check of the message refused the commit, so that one attempt reported the findings of both. Each review is paid for by the user who commits.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the review runs only once the message passes. A commit whose message is refused is not reviewed, since the review would run again once the message is fixed, and the check of the message costs nothing.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement following the owner's decisions of that day: a data record is a RecordType, and a node's address or id is its location.

decisions.ruling: A technical replacement in line with the owner's rulings of the same day on a test's SpecTag and on a draft: a test names its node by its SpecTag, and the check that binds symbols to their nodes reads only the symbols of code other than tests.

children.title: The pre-commit hook
children.reason: On every commit, each check judges the commit in its final form (§s-pcnyfp7gev7syax). So the tools that rewrite files run before the checks, and what the hook generates waits in the working tree until the author stages it, since what a commit holds is its author's choice.
examples: A developer edits a RecordType, an owner approves the new wording, and the developer stages the specification and commits. `sheriff types` generates the RecordType's new types from the staged nodes, and the hook writes them into the working tree and names them. `sheriff binding` refuses the commit, since the staged types differ from what the approved wording produces (§s-dbk2vyeg8z5jxna). The developer stages the new types and commits again. The most likely mistake is to let the checks read the types that `sheriff types` has just written, so that the commit passes with the old types staged.

children.title: The working tree compared with what a push sends
children.text:
Before a push for which the tests are to run (§s-b6qdtghnyha3fhk), the pre-push hook compares the working tree with each commit that the tests judge: each commit that is pointed to, directly or through a tag, by a ref that the push creates or updates, and that meets the conditions under which the tests run.

The hook refuses the push where either of the following holds for a file, and names each such file:
- the file differs between the working tree and such a commit;
- the file is in only one of the two, even where it is a file in the working tree that git does not track.

The hook leaves out the files that git ignores. Where it does not refuse the push, it runs the tests in the working tree.
children.reason: The tests run in the working tree, which holds what each clone installs or builds for itself, so they judge a pushed commit only where the working tree holds what that commit holds.
examples: A developer commits a change and leaves an edit to `src/a.ts` uncommitted. The specification is approved, and the project's own guidelines name a push as the moment at which the tests run. The pre-push hook refuses the push and names `src/a.ts`. The most likely mistake is to run the tests in the working tree as it is, so that they pass or fail because of an edit that the pushed commit does not hold.

decisions.problem: The pre-push hook ran the tests over the working tree, its uncommitted changes and files never added included, while every check reads the commit being made and never what it does not hold.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the push is refused while the working tree differs from what it sends, files it ignores left aside, rather than the hook setting such changes aside itself; then the tests run in the working tree.

children.title: Turning the git hooks on when a session starts
children.text:
In a repository whose root holds `sheriff.config.json`, the agent's hook that runs when a session starts (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw) does the following with git's `core.hooksPath`:
- where it is unset, the hook sets it to `.githooks` in the repository's git configuration and says so;
- where it points to a directory other than `.githooks`, the hook says that the git hooks that `sheriff init` writes (§s-7unxytshhc4md54) do not run.

The hook also names each git hook in `.githooks/` that git's index holds, in either of the following cases:
- git's index holds that git hook without the executable mode;
- on a file system that keeps the executable bit, the git hook's file lacks that bit.

For each such git hook, the agent's hook says how to make the git hook executable on every system: `chmod +x <hook>` and `git update-index --chmod=+x <hook>`, then a commit. It leaves the mode of each file and git's index as they are. It leaves out the project's own tools in `.githooks/<hook>.d/` (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p).
children.reason: In a clone where git does not run the git hooks, no check runs on a commit. A git hook that git does not run cannot report that it was skipped, while the hook that runs when a session starts runs in every clone. The hook that runs when a session starts leaves it to the author of the next commit to record a git hook's mode, since what a commit holds is its author's choice.
examples: A repository set up on Windows has its git hooks committed without the executable mode. A developer clones it on Linux and starts a session. The hook that runs when a session starts names each git hook and says how to make it executable. The most likely mistake is to make the git hooks executable in the working tree without saying so, which leaves the index as it was, so that each of the other clones still gets git hooks that git skips.

decisions.problem: An automated security review found that the plugin's session start turns on whatever hooks `.githooks/` holds in a repository whose root holds `sheriff.config.json`, so a repository someone opens could have git run code it brought, which git never does for a clone until its user turns its hooks on.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the rule stands, and nothing is built against it. The consent that counts is the trust a user gives a folder in Claude Code, before which a plugin the project declares does not load; a repository taking the method runs its own code at every push anyway, since the pre-push hook runs its tests; and the case left open needs together the plugin installed by the user rather than declared by the project, Claude Code run without its dialog of trust, and a clone nobody looked at.

decisions.problem: A repository whose hooks git's index held without the executable mode, as one set up on Windows did, ran none of its checks in a clone on Linux or macOS, git skipping each hook with a hint, and nothing told its user so.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the session start names each git hook git's index holds without the executable mode and, where files keep that bit, each whose file lacks it, says how to make it executable on every system, and changes neither a file's mode nor the index.

decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the group and to option A in all three questions ("A", in answer to "Do you agree to group 8 and to option A in all three questions?").

children.title: The settings of each runner when a session starts
children.text:
In Claude Code, the hook that runs when a session starts writes into the user's git configuration, with `git config --global`, each setting of the runner `claude` (§s-tnz9zgqx8c629a7) that the user has given as an option of the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5). It does so in any repository, whenever the configuration lacks the setting or holds a value different from the option's.

Then, in a repository whose root holds `sheriff.config.json`, the agent's hook that runs when a session starts (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), in Claude Code or in Codex CLI, names each setting of the runner that `sheriff review` would run on a commit there (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u), where the user's git configuration lacks that setting.

That runner is the one that `review.runner` in `sheriff.config.json` names, or otherwise the runner of the SpecSheriff plugin whose tools the git hooks would use there (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p). For each setting, the hook names the default that `sheriff review` uses for it. It asks the agent to do the following:
- to offer the user each default to confirm or replace;
- to write the value that the user gives in reply with `git config --global`, even where that value is the default.

The hook makes this request once for each runner on each machine. After making it, the hook sets `specsheriff.review.claudeAsked` or `specsheriff.review.codexAsked` to `true` in the user's git configuration. The hook stops making the request about a runner once that runner's key is `true`.
children.reason: A run of the reviewer is paid for by the user who commits, so the user who commits chooses the settings of each runner (§s-tnz9zgqx8c629a7), once, as soon as an agent can ask. The git hooks run the reviewer outside the agent, so they read those settings from the user's git configuration, where the hook that runs when a session starts also writes the options that Claude Code asked the user for.
examples: A user installs the plugin for Codex CLI and opens a repository that `sheriff init --agent codex` has set up. The hook that runs when a session starts names `specsheriff.review.codexModel` and `specsheriff.review.codexEffort` with their defaults, and the agent asks the user about them. The user confirms the effort and names a model, and the agent writes both. The most likely mistake is to write the defaults without asking, so that the user pays for settings that the user never chose.

children.title: The agent's hook after an edit
children.reason: The checks run where the agent works, so that a mistake is found at the edit that introduces it (§s-epaw9sgyaajzn8g). They run only where something has changed since they last ran, so that a session that only reads the repository through the shell is not held up.
examples: An agent that has written the test of rule R adds the SpecTag of R to a function in a new file, `src/order.ts`. The hook runs `sheriff reindex`, which adds `src/order.ts` to the `meta.code` of R, and the checks then accept that list. The most likely mistake is to run `sheriff reindex` only where a file under `specs/` has changed, and then `sheriff binding` refuses the `meta.code` of R after an edit to code alone (§s-t383grkn3q68dpf).

decisions.problem: The after-edit hook ran every step after every shell command, a read-only one included, which took most of a minute on a large repository; it missed PowerShell; and the agent was never told a node its edit had left unchecked. The pre-push hook ran the tests of the system's code alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the checks run after an edit only where the last commit or the working tree changed since they last ran, the regeneration only where `specs/` or the settings changed; PowerShell is read as Bash is; each status emptied is reported; the tests of a project's own checks and generators run before a push with the system's.

decisions.problem: The rules of how each check is made (§s-4kd2pave7vm4hmd), confirmed by the owner that day, name what this node did not say.
decisions.ruling: In the owner's name, carrying those rules out: the regeneration after an edit also runs where the code of a project's own generator differs.

decisions.problem: The agent was told of each node whose status the reindex emptied, which would now take in every section and header whose status follows a changed node.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-9kfdycuq34beqvs: the agent is told about each node that `sheriff reindex` made a draft, other than a section or a header.

children.title: Checks run by `sheriff validate`
children.text: How `sheriff validate` checks the specification itself.

children.title: A key written more than once in one object
children.text:
`sheriff validate` refuses each key written more than once in one object, naming the file, the key and the line number of each of its values. Each such refusal also states that `sheriff reindex` merges such values whenever it can keep all of them (§s-w5wg69pvvhedsws).

`sheriff validate` finds a key written more than once by reading as text each file of the specification, of its archive (§s-f2b5zvc565s242f) and of its schema (§s-eferktypcj7njt5) that the repository keeps, the project's extension of the schema included (§s-xm8rz4uupb73gu5). It refuses each of these files whose text is not valid JSON, naming the file and the line at which parsing failed.

Where `sheriff validate` refuses a key or a file, it stops before it runs any check that reads the nodes.
children.reason: A JSON parser keeps one of the values written under a key and silently drops the others, so only the file's text shows a key written more than once.

decisions.problem: Nothing refused a file whose object holds one key twice. JSON Schema leaves the behaviour of such a document undefined, so it escapes the check that it matches its schema (§s-eferktypcj7njt5), and a tool reading it keeps the last of the two values alone.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the check of the specification refuses it, so a commit cannot carry it.

children.title: How the schema of the specification is composed
children.reason: The extensions of the schema are added in a fixed order, so that the composed schema and every refusal are the same on every machine. An extension adds only new names, so that every definition of the SpecSheriff guidelines and of a chosen extension stays as the SpecSheriff guidelines or the chosen extension define it (§s-xm8rz4uupb73gu5). The project's own extension is added last, since its `fields` may set conditions for a kind that a chosen extension adds. The tools stop at a refused extension, since the extensions after it may rely on what it would have added.
examples: A project that has chosen the RecordType extension of the guidelines declares `RecordType` in the `kinds` of its own extension of the schema. The SpecSheriff tools refuse that extension, since the schema of the RecordType extension already defines that kind of node. To add a field to every RecordType, the project declares that field in `fields`, under `RecordType`.

children.title: The chosen extensions and the installed plugin
children.text:
A command of the SpecSheriff tools that reads the chosen extensions of the guidelines (§s-mbmnsnxenmavu3z, §s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) runs only where the installed SpecSheriff plugin delivers each of them (§s-j5qmmdq4m26mdvw). Where the plugin lacks any of them, the command refuses to run. The refusal names each missing extension and the version of the SpecSheriff tools in the plugin. `sheriff reindex` then leaves every file unchanged.

The commands that read the chosen extensions include `sheriff validate`, `sheriff binding` and `sheriff reindex`, which, as they compose the schema of the specification, add to it the schema of each chosen extension that has one (§s-xzcw3hv4hmxz7h7). The commands that read the chosen extensions also include `sheriff guard`, which checks an agent's edit before it is made (§s-st6td4mua9uqt9z). The plugin delivers an extension where the extension's file is at the path given for each extension of the guidelines (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u).

Each command that reads the chosen extensions runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-j5qmmdq4m26mdvw).
children.reason: Without an extension's file, the SpecSheriff tools can neither compose the schema that the extension adds nor run the checks of its table (§s-gpzs5fcxvp6jkrp). A command that ran without the file would accept on one machine what the same command refuses on a machine whose plugin delivers the extension.
examples: A project chooses an extension that a new release of the SpecSheriff plugin delivers. A team member's machine still has an earlier release, which does not deliver it. On that machine, `sheriff validate` refuses to run, naming the extension and the earlier release's version, so the git hook refuses the commit. The most likely mistake is to compose the schema without the missing extension, which lets the command accept, on that machine, a node that the extension's checks would refuse.
