children.title: Validation against the schema before a command works on the files
children.reason:
Each command relies on the structure that the schema defines for a file. Only validation against the schema shows where a file departs from that structure and what is wrong there. `sheriff reindex` builds each file from all the files, so writing only some of them would leave the files inconsistent with one another.

A key written more than once is merged first, since a file read without the merge holds only its last value. What an earlier release wrote is changed first, since the schema refuses its old names. What `sheriff reindex` writes itself is excluded from the validation, since a node written by hand receives it only when `sheriff reindex` runs.

That sentence is inaccurate, since the validation leaves out what the command itself writes.

examples: A cell of a `TableRule` holds a node whose sid was copied from a rule in another file. `sheriff validate` refuses that sid and names both nodes. The easiest mistake to make is to compare only the nodes outside cells, and such a comparison misses this duplicate.

children.title: Terms defined in a domain
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), `sheriff validate` compares the place where each term node (§s-ypa92gpcj3f5zj8) of the base specification is defined with the places of the nodes that cite it or link to it (§s-cb9rbh8q88a84xp). It refuses each of the following:
- a term node in a domain's folder, where a node outside that domain and outside the part of the technical appendix named after that domain cites the term or links to it (§s-8p52mzm3y33cf7z);
- a term node in the contracts section (§s-z6tq6a3btnvvwx7) that at least one node cites or links to, where all such nodes are in a single domain or in the part of the technical appendix named after that domain (§s-qscrdhf6kj57gbx).

A node is in a domain where its file is in the domain's folder, `specs/<domain>/` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). A node is in the part of the technical appendix named after a domain where its file is `specs/tech/<domain>.json` (§s-gvafe6bnstwab8b).

Each refusal names the term node by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx). A refusal of the first kind also names each node that cites the term or links to it from outside the domain and outside the part of the technical appendix named after the domain. A refusal of the second kind names the domain into which the term is to be moved.

`sheriff validate` runs these checks regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-8p52mzm3y33cf7z, §s-qscrdhf6kj57gbx).
children.reason: The place where a term is defined is determined by which nodes cite it or link to it. So only a check that reads every citation and every link in the specification can tell whether a term is in the part that needs it.
examples: The domain `users` defines the term “account”, which only its own rules cite. A commit adds a rule to the domain `requests` that has a `refines` link to that term. `sheriff validate` refuses the term node and names the new rule, until the term is moved to the contracts section. The most likely mistake is to look only at the citations, so that the link from the rule in `requests` goes unnoticed.

children.title: How a node's location is computed
children.text:
The SpecSheriff tools compute a node's location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx) from the path of its file and where the node is in the specification. They compute it for each node of the specification in the files that the repository keeps.

In a file of the guidelines, of the appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8) or of the technical appendix (§s-tj38pvm38nepaf5), the first top-level node of the file takes as its location the file's path under `specs/`, without `.json` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). Such locations include `_guidelines/spec`, `_guidelines/extensions/domains` and `tech/stack`. Where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), a domain's header (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7) takes the domain's name as its location. Every other node's location is one of the following, followed by a slash and the node's place:
- in a file of the guidelines, of the appendix of the tools or of the technical appendix, the location of the first top-level node of that file, as in `_guidelines/spec/1.3.4`;
- in the base specification (§s-5x737t9nee4zgaa), the name of the folder under `specs/` that holds the node's file, as in `base/3.2`, `contracts/1` or `requests/2`.

Every node is numbered except the following:
- a term (§s-khqsmy6mhejkrhg), whose place is the term's name;
- the first top-level node of a file of the guidelines, of the appendix of the tools or of the technical appendix;
- a domain's header.

A numbered node's place is its position among the numbered nodes under its parent, counted from one. Where the parent is numbered too, the parent's place and a dot come before that position, as in `3.2`.

The SpecSheriff tools go through the numbered nodes under a node in the order of the node's children. Under a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6), the nodes in its cells come after its children, row by row through its groups and, within a row, column by column.

In a folder of the base specification, the top-level nodes of its files and the children of a domain's header are treated as nodes under one parent. The SpecSheriff tools go through them file by file, in the code-point order of the files' paths. The top-level nodes of one file come in the order in which the file lists them. The children of a domain's header take the header's position in that order.

In a file of the guidelines, of the appendix of the tools or of the technical appendix, each further top-level node of the file is numbered under the location of the first node, after that node's children.
children.reason: `sheriff reindex` writes the locations that `sheriff validate` checks (§s-ztseyetus7np6br, §s-stxmhq3hgfndvn6). Both commands therefore need one computation that gives every node a location of its own that is the same on every machine.
examples: A domain named `requests` is kept in three files: `specs/requests/00-requests.json` holds its header, `specs/requests/intake.json` holds one section, and `specs/requests/review.json` holds another. The header's location is `requests`, and the sections' locations are `requests/1` and `requests/2`. The fourth node of the second section is a `TableRule`, `requests/2.4`, each of whose rows holds one node, so the node in its third row is `requests/2.4.3`. The most likely mistake is to number each file from one, which gives both sections the location `requests/1`.

children.title: An approved node with no approval in force
children.text:
`sheriff validate` refuses each approved node for which no approval of its current wording is in force (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb, §s-cey3k9xxjvkpyqz). The refusal names the node by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx).

`sheriff validate` checks each node of the specification in the files that the repository keeps, including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6). It leaves out the following nodes, whose approval status `sheriff reindex` derives from other nodes (§s-ztseyetus7np6br):
- each section;
- the header of each domain, where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm, §s-yccuyqbypzzx2gu).
children.reason: A node's approval status is written in its file, where anyone can set it to `approved` by hand. The approval itself is recorded separately from the node, in `specs/_approvals.jsonl` (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb). Comparing the two reveals an approval status typed by hand and one left `approved` after the wording changed.
examples: A person edits the text of an approved rule by hand and commits the change without running `sheriff reindex`. `sheriff validate` refuses the rule, since no approval of its new wording is in force. Had `sheriff reindex` run, it would have made the rule a draft, and the check would have passed.

decisions.problem: A confirmation was compared with the node's one owner at every commit.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-5ah25f6gy99panq: any owner may approve a node, and whether the approver is an owner is judged at the commit that adds the approval.

children.title: Who an added approval names
children.text:
`sheriff validate` accepts an approval (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb) that a commit adds to `specs/_approvals.jsonl` only where both of the following hold:
- its node is in the files that the repository keeps;
- it names an owner of that node (§s-6sk8uet75dmq5qz) as of that commit (§s-acacahc8c9estmr).

`sheriff validate` refuses any other approval that the commit adds. The refusal names the sid and the email address that the approval holds. Where the node is in the files that the repository keeps, the refusal also names the node's file, its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx) and its owners.

An approval is added by a commit where `specs/_approvals.jsonl` holds more lines identical to that approval after the commit than it held in the commit's parent. For a merge commit, the parent is its first parent. `sheriff validate` reads the parent's approvals in the form into which `sheriff reindex` would rewrite them (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv).

`sheriff validate` takes a node's owners from the model of the specification (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx). Of the lines that a commit adds, it checks only approvals.
children.reason: Only a node's owners may approve it, while anyone may withdraw an approval (§s-67vekyup7y8smap, §s-fpq35tf3pehgk64). A node's owners may change from one commit to the next, so each approval is judged against the owners as of the commit that adds it. A later change of owners then leaves the approvals given before it in force.
examples: The nearest section above a rule names `a@example.com` as its owner. A commit adds an approval of the rule by `b@example.com`, and `sheriff validate` refuses it, naming both addresses. A commit that adds the same approval and also makes `b@example.com` an owner of that section is accepted. The most likely mistake is to judge the approval against the owners named in the commit's parent, which would refuse that second commit.

children.title: A removed node and the archive
children.text:
`sheriff validate` checks that a commit adds to the archive (§s-f2b5zvc565s242f) exactly the nodes that it removes from the specification and that must be archived (§s-qb79dcw694x2h63). It checks only the nodes of the files that the repository keeps.

A node is removed by a commit if the parent of the commit holds a node with its sid, and that sid is gone from the specification after the commit. For a merge commit, the parent is its first parent. A removed node must be archived where both of the following hold:
- it has ever been approved (§s-67vekyup7y8smap);
- its approval status is set by approvals, unlike a section's, which is derived from the nodes under it (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs).

`sheriff validate` looks up the approvals of a removed node by the sid that the node has in the parent of the removing commit.

A node of the archive is added by a commit in which the archive after the commit holds more nodes with that node's location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), kind and wording (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq) than the archive of the commit's parent. `sheriff validate` reads the parent's archive in the form into which `sheriff reindex` would rewrite it (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv). For a node in a cell of a `TableRule`, the wording compared is the node's own wording.

The entry of a removed node is a node that the commit adds to the archive with the location, the kind and the wording that the removed node had in the commit's parent. `sheriff validate` accepts the commit only if all of the following hold:
- each removed node that must be archived has its entry in the archive;
- the `archived` field of each such entry gives the date of the removal and the reason for it;
- each node that the commit adds to the archive is the entry of a removed node that must be archived.

When `sheriff validate` refuses a commit, it names the sid of each removed node that the refusal concerns, and the file and the location of each node of the archive that it concerns.
children.reason: The archive keeps each removed rule that the code may have implemented, and nothing else (§s-f2b5zvc565s242f). An archived node has no sid, so the entry of a removed node can be checked only in the commit that removes the node.
examples: A commit removes the approved rule `base/3.2` and the empty section `base/5`. It adds to `specs/_archive/base.json` a `TextRule` that has the location `base/3.2` and the rule's wording, and whose `archived` field gives the date and the reason. The closest mistake is to archive the empty section as well: `sheriff validate` then refuses the commit, naming `specs/_archive/base.json` and `base/5`.

children.title: Validation of a file of the archive
children.text:
`sheriff validate` and `sheriff reindex` validate each file of the archive only against `archive-file.schema.json` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). They do so at the same points at which they validate the files of the specification. `sheriff reindex` does so after it has changed what an earlier release wrote (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv).

The only things that schema requires of a node of the archive are the following:
- it has a location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx) and a kind;
- it has an `archived` field that holds the date of the removal and the reason for it, and may also hold the sid of the node that replaced it (§s-f2b5zvc565s242f);
- it holds no sid, no node under it and no link pointing at it (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz).

The schema admits every other property of the node in any form.

Where the schema refuses a file of the archive, `sheriff validate` and `sheriff reindex` name that file, with every refusal in it. Each of these commands then stops, and `sheriff reindex` leaves every file unchanged.
children.reason: Each SpecSheriff tool that reads the archive relies on the structure of the nodes it reads. A schema limited to that structure checks it while admitting a node that an earlier release archived.

decisions.problem: No row of the main table of checks names the check that a node of the archive holds no sid: row 10.1.3 now covers only the nodes of the specification. The agent treats the validation of a file of the archive as part of row 10.1.11's check that a node is placed in the archive, as the owner's ruling of 2026-11-12 assigned the checks of what the tools read from the archive to rows 10.1.3 and 10.1.11.
decisions.ruling: The owner agreed to the node, with the validation of a file of the archive taken as part of the check of row 10.1.11 of the main table of checks, which therefore stays as agreed ("ok").

children.title: The target of a link
children.text: `sheriff validate` accepts a link only where its target is the sid of a node of the model of the specification (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx, §s-x8usyy38qa56k6a). It refuses any other link declared by a node of the specification in the files that the repository keeps, including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6). The refusal names the node that declares the link by its file, its sid and its location in the specification (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and names the link's type and its target.
children.reason: Only a link whose target is a node of the specification can be followed. Only such a link appears among the links pointing at its target (§s-bpdqd9v72wg7vsz).
examples: A rule still has a `refines` link to a rule that a later commit removed and archived. `sheriff validate` refuses the link, since no node of the specification holds the removed rule's sid any longer. The most likely mistake is to look for the target only among the nodes in the files that the repository keeps. A check that made that mistake would refuse a `refines` link from a rule of a project's own guidelines to a rule of the SpecSheriff guidelines, which the project takes from the SpecSheriff plugin. `sheriff validate` accepts that link.

children.title: Link types reserved for terms
children.text: `sheriff validate` accepts a link of type `term-relation` or `uses` only where both of its ends are term nodes (§s-ypa92gpcj3f5zj8, §s-76dutms9uv6uha2, §s-s79v9mmyw56hgpx). It checks only a link whose target is a node of the model of the specification (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx). The refusal names the node that declares the link by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and names the link's type and its target. It says that the link is to be agreed with the specification's owners.
children.reason: Whether two terms are bound, and how, shows how the entities (§s-9w3u3wn37wksyxd) that they name relate to one another. The specification's owners decide that, so the refusal sends whoever wrote the link to them, rather than suggesting a type.
examples: A term cites another term and declares a `cites` link to it. `sheriff validate` refuses that link and sends the author to the owners. They decide whether the terms are bound by a `term-relation` link, and with which `ratio`, or by a `uses` link.

children.title: The bounds of a range in a ratio
children.text:
`sheriff validate` refuses a link whose ratio (§s-bckzdwd35d2nefa) holds a range whose lower bound is greater than its upper bound, such as `3..1`. It accepts a range whose upper bound is `*`, whatever its lower bound is. The refusal names the node that declares the link by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), names the link's target and quotes the ratio.

`sheriff validate` compares the bounds in the ratio of each link declared by a node of the specification in the files that the repository keeps, including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6).
children.reason: The schema of the specification checks how a ratio is written, but cannot compare the two bounds of a range. A range whose lower bound is greater than its upper bound contains no whole number, so the multiplicity it gives can never be satisfied.
examples: A term declares a `term-relation` link with the ratio `1:3..1`. `sheriff validate` refuses the link and quotes `1:3..1`. It accepts `1:9..10` and `1:5..*`. The most likely mistake in the check is to compare the bounds as text: compared as text, `9` is greater than `10`, so `1:9..10` would be refused.

decisions.problem: Rule s-bckzdwd35d2nefa says that in a range of a ratio the lower bound is not greater than the upper one, while the schema checks only the notation of a ratio and no check compares the bounds.
decisions.ruling: The owner chose to add the check ("А.", in answer to "Добавить ли проверку границ кратности: новую строку таблицы 10.1 и узел описания инструментов в формулировках выше?"), and agreed to the row and the node as they were shown.

The most likely mistake is to count only the nodes in a node's `children`, which leaves out the node in the cell.

Where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), `sheriff validate` accepts a domain only where the domain's files hold exactly one header (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7, §s-ctj5v22yn7wr7n4). A domain's files are those in its folder, `specs/<domain>/` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u).

`sheriff validate` refuses any other domain. The refusal names the domain's folder and, for each header that the domain's files hold, the header's file and sid.
children.reason: A domain may be kept in several files (§s-k73czmpkazcx7mu). So a missing header or a second header shows up only when all of them are read.
examples: The domain `requests` is kept in `specs/requests/00-requests.json` and `specs/requests/intake.json`, and whoever split it opened the second file with a new header as well. `sheriff validate` refuses the domain and names both headers. Once the second file holds only sections, the domain passes.

children.title: A run of words in capitals
children.text:
`sheriff validate` refuses each run of three or more words set in capitals (§s-m6upmfq64kw5h4r, §s-83natrftdsmttsu). The refusal names the run, the property that holds it, and the node by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx).

`sheriff validate` checks each node of the specification in the files that the repository keeps, whatever its approval status. It reads a node's title, text and reason, each string in each member of its `TextRule.list`, and each text cell of a `TableRule` (§s-qeensty237e6mmm, §s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6). It reads a node in a cell of a `TableRule` as it reads any other node.

In the text that `sheriff validate` reads, a word set in capitals is a sequence of two or more consecutive characters that meets each of these conditions:
- each of its characters is a capital letter of any script, a digit or a hyphen;
- the first is a capital letter, and the last is a capital letter or a digit;
- no letter, digit or underscore comes immediately before or after the sequence.

A run is three or more words set in capitals with only spaces or tabs between them. Text in backticks, in straight double quotation marks or in curly double quotation marks (“…”) is not read.
children.reason: The check does not understand the text, so it recognises a phrase set in capitals by its form alone. That form is defined exactly, so that ordinary capitalisation and quotations, which keep the spelling of what they quote (§s-7anvune6h4f6mbr), are never refused.
examples: A rule's text ends with the words “WITHOUT ANY EXCEPTION”, written as part of a sentence, outside backticks and quotation marks. `sheriff validate` refuses the node and names that run. children.title: `consumes` links
children.text: Where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), `sheriff validate` accepts a `consumes` link only where it goes from a domain's header to a section in the files of another domain (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7, §s-rdavpdea67hsntf). A domain's files are those in its folder, `specs/<domain>/` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). `sheriff validate` refuses any other `consumes` link, naming the node that declares it by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and naming the link's target. It checks only a `consumes` link whose target is a node of the model of the specification (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx).
children.reason: The index in a domain's header, and the check for a cycle in which domains use one another, both learn from the `consumes` links which domain uses which section (§s-2r59txnms5serdr, §s-bncp7gtyaukur8e). Any other `consumes` link would make the index wrong or the cycle check give a wrong result.
examples: The header of the domain `requests` declares a `consumes` link to the section of the domain `users` that describes how a user signs in, and `sheriff validate` accepts the link. The most likely mistake is to point the link at the rule in that section that the domain `requests` relies on, in which case `sheriff validate` refuses the link.

The refusal names the rule by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and names the link's type and its target. `sheriff validate` runs this check only in the repository where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). There it reads every node of `specs/_guidelines/spec.json` other than a section, including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6).
children.reason: In the repository where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written, the extensions of the guidelines are kept beside them. A link from a rule of the guidelines to a node of an extension therefore resolves and passes every other check.

children.title: Domains that use one another in a cycle
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), `sheriff validate` refuses a change after which domains use one another in a cycle (§s-bncp7gtyaukur8e). The refusal names the domains of one such cycle, in the order in which each uses the next.

One domain uses another where the header of the first (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7) has a `consumes` link to a section of the second. Domains use one another in a cycle where a chain of domains, each of which uses the next, leads back to the domain that it starts from.

`sheriff validate` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-bncp7gtyaukur8e).
children.reason: Only the `consumes` links of the domains' headers state which domain uses which (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7). A node that relies on what another domain states has a link, of whatever type, to the node of that domain that states it (§s-hr7j7scmfkkjnws). So a check that followed links of every type would refuse changes after which no domains use one another in a cycle.
examples: The header of the domain `requests` has a `consumes` link to a section of the domain `users`. The header of `users` has such a link to a section of `requests`. `sheriff validate` refuses the change and names `requests` and `users`. In another project, only the header of `requests` has a `consumes` link to a section of `users`, and a rule of `users` cites a rule of `requests`. There `sheriff validate` accepts the change. The most likely mistake is to treat that citation as a use of `requests` by `users`.

children.title: A RecordType that refers to a RecordType outside its part of the system
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the RecordType extension (§s-hzuzn8hbq6q9q4s), `sheriff validate` stays silent about a reference from one RecordType (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3) to another only in the following cases (§s-8ht2hn88cu2qwz9):
- from a RecordType outside the contracts section (§s-z6tq6a3btnvvwx7), to a RecordType of its own part of the system or to a fragment of a format (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3, §s-rpkq8y79fwg5k92);
- from a fragment of a format, to another fragment of a format (§s-hn9m9dhxaazjn3y).

`sheriff validate` reports each RecordType that holds a reference of any other kind, naming that RecordType and each RecordType that it refers to by such a reference, each by its sid (§s-rpkq8y79fwg5k92, §s-hn9m9dhxaazjn3y). The change still passes.

A RecordType refers to another RecordType in either of these ways:
- its `schema` (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu) names that RecordType at any depth, by a `$ref` or by an `identifierOf` (§s-4npdup7mjkva69y, §s-qpdnkejr5xzc6j3);
- it has a `refines` link (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm) to that RecordType.

A fragment of a format is a RecordType in the contracts section. Where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), the part of the system that a RecordType belongs to is the domain whose files hold the RecordType. Otherwise, it is the section of `specs/base/` that holds the RecordType and whose location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx) is `base/` followed by a single number. The RecordTypes in `specs/base/` that no such section holds are treated as forming one part of the system together.

`sheriff validate` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-rpkq8y79fwg5k92, §s-hn9m9dhxaazjn3y).
children.reason: A RecordType can refer to another RecordType at any depth within its `schema` and through its `refines` links. So only a check that reads a RecordType's whole `schema` and all its `refines` links finds each reference that breaks the rule on what a RecordType may refer to (§s-8ht2hn88cu2qwz9).
examples: In the domain `requests`, the RecordType of a request has a field `deliveryAddress` with a `$ref` to `address`, a fragment of a format. It also has a field `user` whose `identifierOf` names the RecordType of a user in the domain `users`. `sheriff validate` reports that RecordType, naming it and the RecordType of a user, each by its sid, and lets the change pass. The most likely mistake is to leave the reference in the field `user` unreported because that field holds only an identifier. A field `user` that holds only a user's identifier, with no reference to the RecordType of a user, has the type `string` and no `identifierOf`.

children.title: What a `$ref` within a RecordType names
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the RecordType extension (§s-hzuzn8hbq6q9q4s), `sheriff validate` accepts a `$ref` at any depth within a RecordType's `schema` (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu) only where its value is `#` followed by the sid of a RecordType (§s-4npdup7mjkva69y, §s-axjr5ex3p7ys3nd). It refuses any other `$ref`, naming the RecordType that holds it by its sid and quoting the `$ref`.

`sheriff validate` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-axjr5ex3p7ys3nd).
children.reason: A `$ref` that names no RecordType leaves `sheriff types` unable to generate any file (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b). `sheriff validate` runs on every change, so it finds such a `$ref` even in a project whose stack lists no file of types or RuntimeChecks.

children.title: The level in a domain's header
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), `sheriff validate` accepts a domain's header (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7) that contains a level only where the project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) list that level (§s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4, §s-j3v4y4d3sbmdgfp). A header contains a level as the value of its property `level`.

`sheriff validate` refuses any other header that contains a level, naming the header by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and naming the level. A header that contains no level passes this check.

As with every list in the project's own guidelines, the SpecSheriff tools read the levels in the last approved wording (§s-a8fn72xa782wvbk) of each rule that lists them (§s-t9j29hppag2nren). So a level that is added only by a draft wording is accepted only after that wording is approved.

`sheriff validate` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-j3v4y4d3sbmdgfp).
children.reason: The diagram of the domains places each domain in the row of its level (§s-4azsb49pj6sech8). The order of the levels in the list of levels sets the order of the rows (§s-nkyty4dy9x2v2a4). So a level outside that list has no row.
examples: An approved rule in `project.json` refines the rule about a domain's level and lists the levels `core` and `edge`. `sheriff validate` accepts each header that contains `core` or `edge`, and each header that contains no level. A team member adds `platform` to that rule's list, so the rule becomes a draft. Until the new wording is approved, `sheriff validate` refuses each header that contains `platform`, naming `platform`. The most likely mistake is to take the list from the draft wording.

children.title: What a RecordType variant must agree with
children.reason: A data record holds the fields of its RecordType together with those of the RecordType variant that corresponds to the data record's values (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j). Only where every RecordType variant agrees with its RecordType does each data record have one set of fields that the types and RuntimeChecks generated from the RecordType can describe (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9).
examples: The RecordType `notification` names `channel` in its `chosenBy`, and the values of `channel` are `email` and `app`. It refines `message`, a fragment of a format that declares the field `text`. A RecordType variant in the same section as `notification` refines `notification`, names `email` as the value of `channel` in its `answersTo` and declares `address`, and `sheriff validate` accepts it. Another RecordType variant of `notification` names `sms` as the value of `channel` in its `answersTo` and declares `text`. `sheriff validate` refuses it, since `sms` is not a value of `channel` and `notification` takes `text` from `message`. The most likely mistake is to compare the names of a RecordType variant's fields only with those that `notification` declares in its own `schema`, which overlooks `text`.

decisions.problem: The check of data record variants checked a value only where its choosing field held a list of values, so a variant whose field held none passed with any value; nothing held a variant to the domain declaring its value, and the fields a field of type variant holds were not counted among those a variant inherits.
decisions.ruling: The owner: before the first release, 0.1.0, the tools read such values from the choosing field's own list alone, refuse a value not found there, and hold a variant to the part of the data record holding that field; how a project's own guidelines name another place for such values waits past 0.1.0, and the todo stays. Following the rows of §s-jau82aq9juv9zzh on variants, the row says all the check does.

decisions.problem: The check of data record variants read a value from its choosing field's own list alone, held a variant to the part of the data record, and counted no fields of type variant, and no check followed an identifier to the field it takes its type from.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's rulings of the same day: the row reads the lists that rules of domains define for a field of a data record in contracts (§s-xfu2gpzddjnmgks), keeps a variant in the part of the specification that declares its value, and counts the fields of type variant. A row follows each identifier to the field that identifies its data record. The todo on the other place is resolved.

children.title: `"type": "object"` in a RecordType's `schema`
children.text: Where the project has chosen the RecordType extension (§s-hzuzn8hbq6q9q4s), the schema of that extension requires the `schema` of each RecordType (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu) other than a RecordType variant (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j, §s-c2r9jndrjbtbsv6) to hold `"type": "object"` at its top level (§s-c7zj6mraw8w83py). So, when `sheriff validate` validates the files against the schema of the specification (§s-xzcw3hv4hmxz7h7), it refuses a RecordType whose `schema` lacks `"type": "object"` at its top level.
children.reason: A RecordType's `schema` is the RuntimeCheck of its data records (§s-4npdup7mjkva69y). Without `"type": "object"`, that RuntimeCheck would accept a value that is not an object, such as a string.
examples: A hand-written RecordType `user` has a `schema` that holds `properties` for `name` and `email` and no `type`. `sheriff validate` refuses it. The most likely mistake is to accept it because each of its fields has a schema, so that its RuntimeCheck accepts the string `"Ann"` as a user.

children.title: An identifier followed to its end
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the RecordType extension (§s-hzuzn8hbq6q9q4s), `sheriff validate` accepts a field with `identifierOf` (§s-qpdnkejr5xzc6j3) only where both of the following hold:
- its `identifierOf` holds the sid of a RecordType (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3, §s-4npdup7mjkva69y) that names, in its `identifiedBy`, one of its fields as the field that identifies its data records (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu);
- the chain of identifiers that starts at the field ends in a field without `identifierOf` (§s-cqys6wqrnfzu5ac).

`sheriff validate` refuses any other field with `identifierOf`, naming the RecordType that holds it by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx). The refusal also names the field and each condition that the field fails. It names the field by the JSON Pointer to the field's schema within the RecordType's `schema`, such as `/properties/accounts/items`.

The chain of identifiers that starts at a field goes to the field that identifies the data records of the RecordType that the field's `identifierOf` names. Where that field has `identifierOf` too, the chain goes on in the same way. A chain has no end if it comes back to a field that is already in it.

A RecordType's fields here are those that it declares in its `schema` (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu) and those that it takes through `refines` (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm) from another RecordType. `sheriff validate` runs this check wherever a RecordType's `schema` holds `identifierOf`, at any depth, such as in the schema of the members of a list.

`sheriff validate` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-qpdnkejr5xzc6j3, §s-cqys6wqrnfzu5ac).
children.reason: A field with `identifierOf` takes its type from the field at the end of its chain of identifiers (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu, §s-cqys6wqrnfzu5ac). The types and RuntimeChecks generated from the RecordType that holds the field (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9) can therefore give the field a type only where that chain has an end.
examples: The RecordType `statement` has a field `accountId` whose `identifierOf` names the RecordType `account`. The `identifiedBy` of the RecordType `account` names its field `number`, of type `string`. The chain that starts at `accountId` ends at `number`, and `sheriff validate` accepts the field. The RecordTypes `left` and `right` are each identified by a field whose `identifierOf` names the other RecordType, so the chains that start at those fields never end. `sheriff validate` refuses both fields. The most likely mistake is to follow only the first step of each chain and so accept both fields.

children.title: Where the values of a field with `enum` are collected from
children.reason: A field's values are used by `sheriff reindex`, `sheriff validate`, the check of RecordType variants and `sheriff types` (§s-ztseyetus7np6br, §s-agc6fb3vx46pc23, §s-c2r9jndrjbtbsv6, §s-a8fn72xa782wvbk). children.title: Fields with `enum` that `sheriff validate` accepts
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the RecordType extension (§s-hzuzn8hbq6q9q4s), `sheriff validate` accepts a field with `enum` (§s-xfu2gpzddjnmgks) only where both of the following hold:
- its source gives it at least one value when the SpecSheriff tools collect its values (§s-5nf87c3e3jg9v7c, §s-buug8n5eh7tdnsv);
- where its `enumSource.from` is `kind`, its `enumSource.kind` names one of the kinds of node that the project's extension of the schema adds in its field `kinds` (§s-xm8rz4uupb73gu5, §s-hcgmz4v5avbj3nt).

`sheriff validate` refuses any other field with `enum`, naming the RecordType that holds it by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx). The refusal also names the field, each condition that the field fails and, where the field fails the condition on the kind, the kind. It names the field by the JSON Pointer to the field's schema within the RecordType's `schema`, such as `/properties/accounts/items`.

When `sheriff validate` validates the files against the schema of the specification, it refuses a field whose own `enum` holds a value more than once (§s-xzcw3hv4hmxz7h7, §s-upj45kydz8727be). The schema of the RecordType extension requires each `enum` within a RecordType's `schema` (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu) to hold each value only once.

`sheriff validate` checks each field with `enum` at any depth within the `schema` of each RecordType in the files that the repository keeps. It runs these checks regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-upj45kydz8727be, §s-buug8n5eh7tdnsv, §s-hcgmz4v5avbj3nt).
children.reason: The types and RuntimeChecks of a field are generated from its values (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9). So, if `sheriff validate` accepted a field that has no values, or whose values break the rules about their source (§s-xfu2gpzddjnmgks, §s-mt6auv3jz8m5gzh), the types and RuntimeChecks generated from that field's values would inherit the field's defect.
examples: The RecordType of a job log entry has a field `step` whose `enumSource.from` is `kind` and whose `enumSource.kind` is `TextRule`. `sheriff validate` refuses the field and names `TextRule`. Once `enumSource.kind` names `jobStep`, a kind that the project's extension of the schema adds, and the base specification holds a node of that kind, the field passes. The most likely mistake is to accept `TextRule` because the schema of the SpecSheriff guidelines defines it.

children.title: The meta-schema of a RecordType's `schema`
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the RecordType extension (§s-hzuzn8hbq6q9q4s), the schema of that extension validates the `schema` of each RecordType (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu) against a meta-schema of SpecSheriff's own, to which it refers by a `$ref`. The SpecSheriff tools keep that meta-schema in the file `recordtype-meta.schema.json`, in the same folder as that schema (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). The meta-schema's `$id` is `recordtype-meta.schema.json`.

The meta-schema's `$vocabulary` declares the vocabularies of JSON Schema 2020-12 and a vocabulary of SpecSheriff's own, `https://github.com/non4me/SpecSheriff/vocab/recordtype`, which holds the keywords `identifierOf` and `enumSource` (§s-4npdup7mjkva69y, §s-5nf87c3e3jg9v7c).

The meta-schema's `$vocabulary` marks SpecSheriff's vocabulary as optional by giving it the value `false`. So a JSON Schema tool that takes the meta-schema as the meta-schema of a RecordType's `schema`, but does not know that vocabulary, still processes that `schema`.

At any depth within a RecordType's `schema`, the meta-schema checks the value of each of these keywords as the schema of the RecordType extension defines it, and every other keyword as JSON Schema 2020-12 does.
children.reason: The JSON Schema project has announced that its next release will refuse a keyword that no declared vocabulary defines. Declared in a vocabulary of SpecSheriff's own, `identifierOf` and `enumSource` stay valid keywords of a RecordType's `schema` without the prefix `x-`.
examples: A JSON Schema tool that has loaded the meta-schema reads the `schema` of a RecordType whose field `part` holds `enumSource`, and reports no unknown keyword. The most likely mistake is to leave the schema of the RecordType extension referring to the meta-schema of JSON Schema 2020-12, under which no declared vocabulary defines `enumSource`.

children.title: An object in a list
children.text:
`sheriff validate` accepts a member of a `TextRule.list` (§s-eferktypcj7njt5) that is an object only where `TextRule.list.property` names a property and the member holds that property (§s-yuu4ccgch68yzxb). It refuses any other such member. The refusal names the node by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), the member's position in the list and, where the list names one, the property.

`sheriff validate` checks each node of the specification in the files that the repository keeps, including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6). It runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-yuu4ccgch68yzxb).
children.reason: The value of a member that is an object is the value of the property that `TextRule.list.property` names. `sheriff binding` compares that value with the schema or the symbol to which the list points (§s-5hb9k2e34dgn284), so a member without that property has no value to compare.
examples: A rule lists the roles of a user as objects, and its `TextRule.list.property` is `name`. One member is `{"title": "operator"}`. `sheriff validate` refuses that member and names `name`. The most likely mistake is to take the member's only property as its value.

children.title: Files of the technical appendix named after the domains
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), `sheriff validate` accepts a JSON file at any depth in `specs/tech/` only where it is one of the following (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u, §s-vghy37e3p2325ah):

children.title: Sections of the technical appendix matched to the base specification
children.text:
`sheriff validate` accepts each section of the technical appendix (§s-tj38pvm38nepaf5) only where its path of titles is also the path of titles of a section of the base specification (§s-qmmzf9nksfsa3qp, §s-ujnb23vbw3y8cne). It skips the sections of `specs/tech/stack.json` and `specs/tech/debt.json`, the files that hold the stack section and the technical debt section (§s-vj7ercem526zd6v).

The path of titles of a section consists of the titles of the sections that hold it, from the top down, followed by the section's own title. In each file of the technical appendix, each top-level node after the first is treated as a node under the first, as in the computation of locations (§s-ygg5kpcxgzq3m7w).

Where a file of the technical appendix, `specs/tech/<folder>.json`, is named after a folder of the base specification (§s-5x737t9nee4zgaa), its first top-level node represents that folder. So the path of titles of a section of that file starts below that node, and `sheriff validate` looks for the section with the same path of titles in that folder. `sheriff validate` also skips that node itself.

In a folder of the base specification, the path of titles of a section starts with the title of a section that is a top-level node of one of the folder's files. Where the folder is a domain's (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), it may also start with the title of a child of that domain's header (§s-yggv9myedprnaa7).

`sheriff validate` refuses any other section of the technical appendix, naming it by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and giving its title.

`sheriff validate` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-ujnb23vbw3y8cne).
children.reason: To find how a rule is implemented, a reader looks in the technical appendix and follows the same path of titles that leads to the rule in the base specification (§s-vj7ercem526zd6v). A section that matches no section of the base specification holds an implementation that the reader will not find.
examples: The domain `requests` has a section titled “Intake”, which holds a section titled “Validation”. In `specs/tech/requests.json`, the file's first top-level node holds a section titled “Intake”, which holds a section titled “Validation”, and `sheriff validate` accepts both. Another section titled “Validation” is directly under the file's first top-level node, and `sheriff validate` refuses it. The most likely mistake is to accept that section because the domain has a section titled “Validation”, although the domain's section is under “Intake”.

children.title: How a project's own check is run
children.text:
Where a check that a project's own guidelines add (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m) fails, `sheriff validate` refuses the change. Where the rule that lists the check says that the check's failure is only reported, `sheriff validate` reports the failure instead (§s-ujm7nfxkk9j3464). The refusal or the report names the check and shows what the check printed to its standard output and its standard error. Where the check printed nothing, the refusal or the report shows the check's exit status.

`sheriff validate` runs each of the project's own checks with the command that `sheriff.config.json` names for it (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). The check runs in the directory in which `sheriff validate` runs. At a commit, that directory holds what the commit contains (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw). On its standard input, the check receives the model of the specification in the form that `sheriff json` prints (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx). A check passes only if its process exits with status zero.

In its `TextRule.list` (§s-eferktypcj7njt5), the rule that `sheriff.config.json` names for a check lists the check as a member whose value (§s-5hb9k2e34dgn284) is the check's name. `sheriff validate` reads that rule in its last approved wording (§s-a8fn72xa782wvbk). Where the rule, in that wording, lists no member whose value is the check's name, `sheriff validate` refuses the change. The refusal names the check and the rule, and says that the rule's last approved wording does not list the check.

Where the member that lists the check is an object whose `onFailure` is `reported`, the rule says that the check's failure is only reported. Where that member's `onFailure` is `reportedUnlessStrict`, the rule says that, while the specification's `strict` flag (§s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2) is off, the check's failure is only reported. `sheriff validate` reads the flag from the model of the specification that it gives the check.

`sheriff validate` runs the project's own checks only after the files of the specification have passed the check for a key written more than once (§s-7zqsstgnuc772ba) and the validation against their schema (§s-xzcw3hv4hmxz7h7). It runs them before the rest of its checks (§s-pcnyfp7gev7syax). It runs the rest of its checks regardless of what the project's own checks find.

`sheriff validate` refuses the change where one of the project's own checks adds, changes or removes a file in the directory in which the check runs, other than a file that git ignores (§s-vj67ztqkuhxbv7s). The refusal names the check and each such file.

With the option `--strict`, `sheriff validate` gives each of the project's own checks a model of the specification in which the specification is approved and the specification's `strict` flag is on (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2, §s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2). It does so regardless of how the entries in `sheriff.config.json` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u) set the approval status and the flag. The other checks of `sheriff validate` give the same results with or without the option.

`sheriff validate` runs the project's own checks regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-ujm7nfxkk9j3464).
children.reason: Whenever `sheriff validate` runs the checks that the SpecSheriff guidelines require, it also runs a project's own checks, on the same files. Such a check therefore binds every participant, rather than depending on someone remembering to run it (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m).
examples: The rule that lists the project's own checks has `name` as its `TextRule.list.property`, and one of its members is `{"name": "spelling", "onFailure": "reported"}`. The check `spelling` finds a misspelt word in a node's text, prints the node's sid and exits with status 1. `sheriff validate` reports the failure, showing the sid, and the commit passes. The most likely mistake is to refuse the commit because the check's exit status is not zero.

The member that lists the check `spelling` is `{"name": "spelling", "onFailure": "reportedUnlessStrict"}`. While the `strict` flag is off, `sheriff validate` reports each misspelt word, and the commit passes. An owner runs `sheriff settings strict on`, and the check fails when `sheriff validate --strict` runs it, so `sheriff settings` refuses to turn the flag on and names `sheriff validate --strict`. The most likely mistake is to read the flag from the entries in `sheriff.config.json` rather than from the model that the check receives. With that mistake, the flag is turned on, and the next commit is refused because of that check.

children.title: Checks run by `sheriff binding`
children.text: How `sheriff binding` makes each of its checks.

children.title: What a commit adds, changes and removes in the code and the tests
children.text:
The SpecSheriff tools find what a commit adds, changes and removes in the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc), including its tests. They compare each file as the commit leaves it with the same file in the commit's parent. For a merge commit, the parent is its first parent. The first commit of a repository is compared with an empty repository. A file that the commit moves or renames is compared with the file at its earlier path. A line that the commit adds or removes is one that git shows as added or removed when it compares the two versions of the file with the Myers algorithm, git's default, however git is configured on the machine.

A commit changes only the symbols (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4), the files bound as a whole (§s-5qdjyf6t898rsd4, §s-trwczfskj5zmuft) and the tests (§s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc) that both the commit's parent and the commit hold. It adds each of them that only the commit holds. It removes each of them that only the commit's parent holds.

A commit changes a symbol, a test or a file bound as a whole where its two versions differ (§s-u6mj5yv8ngnz79v). A symbol or a test extends from its first line to its last, including its decorators. So a change in a nested symbol also changes each symbol that encloses it.

In each file of the system's code other than tests, if a description covers the file's language (§s-33fw3ga4ctd94dq), the SpecSheriff tools treat the code outside every symbol, other than imports, as one more symbol of that file. That symbol holds that code alone. A finding names it by the file alone.

A symbol or a test in the commit's parent is the same as the one with the same name, nested in symbols with the same names, in the file as the commit leaves it. A test that the commit renames, keeping its SpecTag and changing nothing else in it, also stays the same test (§s-8xw4mgvpexyvw5q, §s-9j2mmnuuwmx5ksn).

A commit also changes each symbol, each file bound as a whole and each test whose SpecTags it changes (§s-9j2mmnuuwmx5ksn). A commit changes the SpecTags of a symbol, file or test where at least one SpecTag binds it in the commit's parent but not after the commit, or after the commit but not in its parent. Two SpecTags are the same only where their texts are the same, including the text after `@spec none` (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp).

A commit adds an entry in the bindings file (§s-trwczfskj5zmuft) where the commit's parent holds no entry for the same file. It changes an entry whose SpecTags differ from those of the same file's entry in the parent.

A commit adds or changes each SpecTag of the following kinds:
- a SpecTag on a line that the commit adds;
- a SpecTag in an entry that the commit adds or changes.

Neither kind includes a SpecTag that binds the same symbol, file or test and has the same text as the SpecTag that binds it in the commit's parent.

A commit leaves unchanged each symbol, each file bound as a whole and each test that remains in the repository and that the commit neither adds nor changes.
children.reason: The checks that run on a commit judge code and tests according to whether the commit adds, changes, removes or leaves them unchanged. A single definition of each of these lets every check judge the same code and tests in the same way.
examples: A commit deletes the line `log(id);` inside the function `close` and changes nothing else in it. The version of `close` in the commit's parent contains that line, so the two versions produce different syntax trees, and the commit changes `close`. The most likely mistake is to look only at the lines that the commit adds, which misses a change made by deleting lines.

A commit rewords a comment in a stylesheet bound by SpecTags at its start and changes nothing else in it. The SpecSheriff tools parse both versions with the grammar of CSS and leave the comment out of both trees. The trees are the same, so the commit does not change the stylesheet's code. The most likely mistake is to count any change to the text of a file bound as a whole as a change to its code.

todos.text: A git repository nested in the working tree, such as a worktree kept inside the project, is a directory that git does not list as a file of the commit. No rule says that the SpecSheriff tools do not read such a repository as a file, so the test that checked it was removed. A rule on which files the SpecSheriff tools read in the working tree would allow that test to be restored.

children.title: How two versions of code are compared
children.reason: A change to the code makes the SpecSheriff tools check that code against its rules again (§s-9j2mmnuuwmx5ksn). A syntax tree keeps whatever can alter what the code does and drops the whitespace to which the language gives no meaning. So comparing trees treats as changes exactly the edits that can affect what the code does. Where the SpecSheriff tools have no grammar for a file's language, comparing the text treats every edit as a change, so that no change to the code passes unchecked.
examples: A commit re-wraps the call `send(to, subject, body);` onto three lines and adds a comment above it. Both versions produce the same syntax tree, so the commit changes no code. The most likely mistake is to compare the lines, which counts the re-wrapped call as a change.

A commit renames the test `@spec s-… refuses an empty name` to `@spec s-… refuses a blank name` and changes nothing else in it. With the test's name left out, both versions produce the same tree, so the commit leaves the test unchanged. The most likely mistake is to keep the test's name in the tree, which counts the renamed test as changed.

A commit indents the key `retries` by two more spaces in a YAML file bound as a whole, which nests the key under the key above it. The grammar of YAML makes indentation part of the syntax, so the two versions produce different trees, and the commit changes the file. The most likely mistake is to compare only the tokens, which lets the nested key pass as unchanged.

children.title: A SpecTag that names no node
children.text:
`sheriff binding` accepts a SpecTag `@spec <sid>` (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) only where its sid names a node of the model of the specification (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx) as the commit leaves it. It checks each such SpecTag in the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc), including the tests, and in the bindings file (§s-trwczfskj5zmuft). It refuses a SpecTag whose sid names no node of that model, naming the file, the line and the sid (§s-w4g56n2bs753rt3).

`sheriff binding` refuses a SpecTag whose sid names no node at every commit, whether or not:
- the commit changes the code or the test that the SpecTag is meant to bind;
- the specification is approved.
children.reason: Once a node is removed, every SpecTag that names it binds its code or test to nothing, wherever that SpecTag is placed.
examples: A rule is removed, while a function elsewhere still carries its SpecTag. The commit that removes the rule changes no code, and `sheriff binding` refuses the SpecTag on the function. The most likely mistake is to check only the SpecTags on code that the commit changes, which lets the SpecTag pass until someone edits the function.

children.title: Code and tests outside the commit that no SpecTag binds
children.text:
`sheriff binding` treats each of the following that the commit leaves unchanged (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2) as the rule requires (§s-kkbqcb9xrpaepwn) for code and tests that no SpecTag (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) binds:
- in the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) other than tests, a symbol (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4), the code outside every symbol of a file (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2) or a file to be bound as a whole (§s-5qdjyf6t898rsd4, §s-trwczfskj5zmuft) that no SpecTag binds (§s-9rtrj24myzjvshu);
- a test of the system's code that declares no SpecTag (§s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc), or whose SpecTag names a node that is not a rule (§s-utf4mbt7ref8g9c).

`sheriff binding` takes the specification's approval status and its `strict` flag as the commit leaves them (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2, §s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2).
children.reason: The approval status and the `strict` flag decide what code that is outside the commit, and that no SpecTag binds, costs the commit: nothing, a warning or a refusal. The commit itself may change either of them.
examples: A commit adds the entry that approves the specification while its `strict` flag is off, and old code elsewhere carries no SpecTag. The commit is judged against the specification as the commit leaves it, approved, so the commit passes with a warning. The most likely mistake is to judge the commit by the status before it, a draft, which lets the commit that approves the specification pass without the warning.

children.title: The code and the tests of a draft rule
children.text:
`sheriff binding` refuses a commit that adds, changes or removes (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2) code or a test bound by a SpecTag (§s-8xw4mgvpexyvw5q) that names a draft rule (§s-wpadgy2budcxa3v). It does so regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug).

The refusal names the rule by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx). It also names each symbol (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4) and each test concerned, with its file and its line, and each other file concerned. Where the commit removes a symbol or a test, its line is read in the commit's parent.

`sheriff binding` reads the SpecTags both in the commit's parent and in the code and the tests as the commit leaves them. From the specification as the commit leaves it, `sheriff binding` takes the approval status of each rule that those SpecTags name. A rule here is a node of one of the kinds that the node on the form of a SpecTag lists (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp).
children.reason: A draft rule may still be incomplete or wrong, so code or a test written, changed or removed for it would follow a wording that no owner has approved (§s-utvqbypzhmgndug).
examples: A rule that a function implements is reworded and becomes a draft. Before an owner approves the new wording, a commit deletes the function. `sheriff binding` refuses the commit and names the rule. The most likely mistake is to read the SpecTags only as the commit leaves the code, which lets the deletion pass, since no SpecTag naming the rule is left.

children.title: Entries that only an owner of the specification records
children.text:
For a setting that only an owner of the specification changes (§s-chsfpkgpmfk4fft), `sheriff binding` accepts a commit's change to the entries in `sheriff.config.json` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u) only where both of the following hold:
- after the commit, the entries for that setting begin with all those that the commit's parent holds for it, unchanged and in the same order;
- each entry that follows them names an owner of the specification (§s-6sk8uet75dmq5qz).

`sheriff binding` refuses every other change to the entries for a setting that only an owner of the specification changes. The refusal names the setting, each entry concerned and the specification's owners.

`sheriff binding` reads the entries of the commit's parent in the form into which `sheriff reindex` would rewrite them (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv). For a merge commit, the parent is its first parent. `sheriff binding` takes the specification's owners from `project.json` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u) as the commit leaves it.

`sheriff binding` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-pa8t49pqpwscuq7, §s-y5w6xwvwh857azx, §s-dxzq5rd6eeteza4).
children.reason: Removing, editing or moving an entry already recorded, or recording an entry in the name of a person who is not an owner, could change a setting that only an owner of the specification changes without an act of an owner (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2, §s-q3pfzyaxvpr2zj2, §s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g).
examples: The latest entry for the specification's approval status approves the specification, and the entry before it returned the specification to draft. A person deletes the latest entry by hand, so that the specification would be a draft again. `sheriff binding` refuses the commit, since the first entries for that setting are no longer those of the commit's parent. The most likely mistake is to check only the added entries, which lets the commit return the specification to draft without an owner's entry.

children.title: The SpecTags the tests carry
children.text:
`sheriff binding` refuses each of the following tests of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc), whether the specification is approved or a draft:
- a test that the commit adds or changes (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2) and that declares no SpecTag (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) in the place set for the test's language (§s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc, §s-ay6wntm2dxcgpnp);
- a test that the commit adds or changes and whose SpecTag names a node of the model of the specification (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx) that is not a rule (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp).

Each refusal names the test, its file and its line.

A test whose name or mark holds a bare sid (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv) declares no SpecTag. The refusal of such a test names `sheriff reindex`, which writes the SpecTag.

`sheriff binding` reads the tests in each file that the glob patterns for tests in `sheriff.config.json` match, where a description covers the file's language (§s-33fw3ga4ctd94dq). For a test that the commit leaves unchanged and that declares no SpecTag, or whose SpecTag names a node that is not a rule, the check of code and tests outside the commit applies instead (§s-3xx2eukc8gtd2tx).
children.reason: A test counts toward the rule that its SpecTag names when the SpecSheriff tools judge whether that rule is implemented (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf). A test with no SpecTag, or with one that names a section or a term, counts toward no rule.
examples: A commit adds a test that begins its name with `@spec s-…`, where the sid is that of the term `request`. `sheriff binding` refuses the test, since a term is not a rule. The most likely mistake is to accept the test because the term exists.

children.title: A test for each rule whose code a commit changes
children.text:
`sheriff binding` accepts a commit that adds or changes code bound to a rule (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4, §s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) only where a test of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) declares that rule's SpecTag (§s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc, §s-m82tz4mp3f9r3fg). It refuses any commit that does not meet this condition, naming the rule by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx).

In this check, the code means the symbols (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4) and the files bound as a whole (§s-5qdjyf6t898rsd4, §s-trwczfskj5zmuft) that the commit adds or changes (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2), other than tests. A rule is bound to such code where one of the code's SpecTags names the rule.

In this check, `sheriff binding` takes into account each test as the commit leaves it, including:
- a test that the commit leaves unchanged;
- a test marked as skipped or as expected to fail.

`sheriff binding` runs this check whether the specification is approved or a draft.
children.reason: A rule's test is written before its code (§s-rah8b37kytb682y). So code added or changed for a rule that no test names was written before the rule's test, or without one.
examples: A commit adds a function whose SpecTag names a rule, and no test in the repository declares that rule's SpecTag. `sheriff binding` refuses the commit and names the rule. The most likely mistake is to look for the test only among the tests that the commit changes, in which case `sheriff binding` refuses a commit whose test was committed earlier.

children.title: A node's `meta.code` and `meta.tests`
children.text:
`sheriff binding` refuses each node whose `meta.code` or `meta.tests` (§s-rwqzepmrt77rv35) differs from the list that `sheriff reindex` would write there (§s-ztseyetus7np6br) from the SpecTags (§s-8xw4mgvpexyvw5q) as the commit leaves the code and the tests (§s-tqdmk6jakx97wra). The refusal names the node by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and gives that list.

`sheriff binding` compares the entries of a node's `meta.code` and `meta.tests` regardless of their order. It checks each node of the specification in the files that the repository keeps, including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6). It runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-tqdmk6jakx97wra).
children.reason: `sheriff reindex` writes a node's `meta.code` and `meta.tests` from the SpecTags (§s-ztseyetus7np6br), but a person may edit them by hand or commit without running it. A list that differs from the SpecTags would show a reader code or tests that are not bound to the node, or would hide some that are.
examples: Rule R is implemented by the function `render` in `src/page.ts` and by `src/texts.json`, which the bindings file binds to R. The `meta.code` of R names both files, and `sheriff binding` accepts it. The most likely mistake is to take into account only the SpecTags placed above symbols, which would make `sheriff binding` refuse that `meta.code` for naming `src/texts.json`.

children.title: A list and its declaration
children.text:
`sheriff binding` accepts a `TextRule.list` (§s-eferktypcj7njt5) only where each of the following holds (§s-f5mm7tagez38ffz):
- where the list has a `TextRule.list.jsonSchema`, each of its values is valid, under JSON Schema 2020-12, against the schema at the place to which that property points;
- where the schema at that place holds the keyword `enum`, directly or through `$ref`, each value of that `enum` is one of the list's values;
- where the list has a `TextRule.list.valueList`, the symbol (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4) to which that property points declares exactly the list's values.

`sheriff binding` refuses every other `TextRule.list`, naming the node by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and naming each value concerned. Where the file to which the list points, the place in it or the symbol cannot be found, the refusal names the one that cannot be found.

Each member of a list gives one of the list's values. The value of a member that is an object is the value of the member's property that `TextRule.list.property` names. `sheriff binding` checks a list only where each of its members that is an object holds that property, which the check of an object in a list requires (§s-cdachayybfvg4na).

A symbol declares the text of each string literal within its lines, as the SpecSheriff tools read a file whose language a description covers (§s-33fw3ga4ctd94dq). A value of the list matches such a literal where the value, written as text, is the literal's text.

`sheriff binding` checks the list of each node of the specification in the files that the repository keeps, including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6). `sheriff binding` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-f5mm7tagez38ffz).
children.reason: A rule's list and the schema or the code that declares the same values are written separately, so either can gain or lose a value unnoticed. Comparing them at every commit keeps the values that the system accepts in line with those that the rule states.
examples: A rule lists the states of a request: `open`, `done` and `cancelled`. The rule's `TextRule.list.jsonSchema` points to `#/properties/state` in `schema/request.schema.json`, and the schema at that place holds `"enum": ["open", "done", "cancelled", "held"]`. `sheriff binding` refuses the list and names `held`, a value of the `enum` that the list does not hold. The most likely mistake is to check only that each value of the list is valid against the schema. All three are, so a state that the schema accepts and the rule does not state would pass.

children.reason: A project's own kind of node is declared in the extension of the schema, which nobody approves, but listed in a rule, which an owner approves (§s-hhnahzmhahf8jht). Comparing the two keeps the declaration of each kind, including whether its nodes require an implementation in code, in line with what an owner has approved.

The commit would then pass, although the rule says that the nodes of the kind `procedure` require no code and the schema says that they do.

children.title: A node's location outside the specification
children.text:
`sheriff binding` refuses each location of a node (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx) written in a file that the repository keeps outside `specs/`, the folder that holds the files of the specification (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u, §s-u5hfbygfyqv4wmf). The refusal names the file, the line and the location, and says that a node is cited by its sid (§s-9spq78kdwsxr759).

`sheriff binding` treats each of the following as a location, regardless of letter case:
- text in the form of a numbered node's location (§s-ygg5kpcxgzq3m7w), such as `base/3.2` or `_guidelines/spec/1.3.4`, whether or not a node is at that location now;
- the location that the model of the specification (§s-w6gybeqn2ttydqx) assigns to a term (§s-khqsmy6mhejkrhg), such as `contracts/request`;
- the location that the model of the specification assigns to the first top-level node of a file of the guidelines, of the appendix of the tools (§s-a4rbry4hsu34hy8) or of the technical appendix (§s-tj38pvm38nepaf5), such as `tech/stack`.

Text has the form of a numbered node's location where it consists of one of the following, followed by a slash and one or more numbers separated by dots:
- the name of a folder under `specs/` that holds files of the base specification (§s-5x737t9nee4zgaa);
- the location of the first top-level node of a file of the guidelines, of the appendix of the tools or of the technical appendix.

`sheriff binding` treats text as a location only where the text stands alone, not as part of a longer path or name, such as `tech/stack` within `specs/tech/stack.json`.

`sheriff binding` leaves out each file that the project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) list as a fixture of the tests of a check that reads citations or locations (§s-6hha5en226aj8hu).

`sheriff binding` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-u5hfbygfyqv4wmf).
children.reason: A node's location can change whenever the specification is reordered, while its sid never changes (§s-9spq78kdwsxr759). Outside the specification, a location comes with no link to the node that it names. After a reordering, a location left in a file would point to another node, or to none, and no other check would notice it.
examples: A guide in `docs/` says “see `base/3.2`”. `sheriff binding` refuses `base/3.2` in that guide, naming the guide, the line and `base/3.2`, even though no node is at that location now. The most likely mistake is to refuse only a location at which a node exists, which lets a location left behind by a removed node pass.

children.title: A citation or a SpecTag outside the specification
children.reason: Outside the specification, a citation or a SpecTag comes with no link to the node that it names (§s-cxtt6jvhqcey2k9). So a sid that names no node, a SpecTag that names anything but a rule of the guidelines (§s-sfjka4zc4rhfu67), or a number in place of a sid would mislead every reader, and no other check would notice any of them.

The most likely mistake is to read only the files that the commit changes, which lets the citation pass until someone edits the guide.

children.title: An edit judged before it is made
children.text:
`sheriff guard` refuses each of the following edits by an agent (§s-83ev4wwesbwnhnp), regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft:
- an edit after which a node that it adds, or a node whose wording (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq) or approval status (§s-tgrnpagrb58tya7) it changes, has the status `approved` while no approval of that node's wording is in force (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb);
- an edit that adds or changes code bound to a rule (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4, §s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp), other than tests, while no test of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) declares that rule's SpecTag (§s-zrsc6asgmhv8tnc);
- an edit to `specs/_approvals.jsonl`, whatever it changes;
- an edit that adds, changes or removes an entry in one of the lists `approvalStatus`, `strict` and `extensions` of `sheriff.config.json` (§s-d3nkw9b6mn98vuw).

The refusal names each such node by its file, its sid and its location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx), and each such rule by its sid and its location. Where a test names such a rule only by a bare sid (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv), the refusal also names `sheriff reindex`, which writes the test's SpecTag.

For an edit to `specs/_approvals.jsonl`, the refusal names `sheriff approve`, which records approvals and their withdrawals (§s-upkur92ry6332y5, §s-xybjqp2rxh8gszf). For an edit to an entry of `approvalStatus`, `strict` or `extensions`, it names that list and `sheriff settings` (§s-chsfpkgpmfk4fft).

While the installed SpecSheriff plugin lacks an extension of the guidelines that the project has chosen, `sheriff guard` refuses every edit, and names each missing extension and the version of the SpecSheriff tools in the plugin (§s-mhsb6fjsq5xn6c9).

`sheriff guard` judges an edit made with Claude Code's `Write`, `Edit` or `MultiEdit`, and a patch that Codex's `apply_patch` applies (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x). It reads the edit, as the agent's harness describes it, from its standard input. It builds in memory each file as the edit would leave it. Where an edit made with `Edit` or `MultiEdit` would not apply, for example where it names text that the file does not contain, `sheriff guard` lets the tool refuse it.

`sheriff guard` judges the nodes in the files that the repository keeps, including a node in a cell of a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6). It leaves out each node whose approval status is derived from other nodes, such as a section (§s-9kfdycuq34beqvs). A file of the specification that would be invalid JSON after the edit is left to the checks that run after the edit (§s-hcmpjmwtgfwzncu).

`sheriff guard` finds the code that an edit adds or changes in the same way as the SpecSheriff tools find what a commit adds or changes (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2), comparing each file as it is with the file as the edit would leave it. Among the tests of the working tree as the edit would leave it, it looks for a test that declares the SpecTag of the rule to which that code is bound.

`sheriff guard` reads the lists `approvalStatus`, `strict` and `extensions` from `sheriff.config.json` as it is now and as the edit would leave it. Where `sheriff.config.json` is missing or is not valid JSON, `sheriff guard` treats each of those lists as empty.

Where it refuses an edit, `sheriff guard` writes the refusal to its standard error and exits with code 2.
children.reason: `sheriff guard` judges each file as the edit would leave it, so that an edit that the rule on an agent's edit forbids is refused before anything is written (§s-83ev4wwesbwnhnp). It judges only the nodes and the code that the edit adds or changes, so that a node or code that the edit leaves as it was never blocks the edit.
examples: An owner asks the agent to approve the specification, and the agent tries to add an entry to `approvalStatus` in `sheriff.config.json` with a file-editing tool. `sheriff guard` refuses the edit and names `approvalStatus` and `sheriff settings`, and the agent runs `sheriff settings status approved`. The most likely mistake is to judge only the files under `specs/`, so that the entry is written without `sheriff settings`, which checks that whoever records it is an owner.
