children.title: The nodes that a commit message must name
children.text:
`sheriff commit-message` accepts a commit message only where it contains the sid of each node to which a SpecTag (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) binds code that the commit adds or changes (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2, §s-7sk3s553ukzwtbm). It refuses any other message. For each node whose sid the message lacks, the refusal names the node's file, sid and location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx).

This check counts as code the following parts of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc), other than tests: the symbols (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4), the code outside every symbol that the SpecSheriff tools treat as one more symbol (§s-2x58az67bm6cxq2), and the files bound as a whole (§s-5qdjyf6t898rsd4, §s-trwczfskj5zmuft). `sheriff commit-message` reads their SpecTags as the commit leaves them.

A message contains a node's sid where the sid appears anywhere in the message. `sheriff commit-message` ignores each line of the message that starts with git's comment character (`core.commentChar`, by default `#`). It also ignores the scissors line that `git commit --verbose` writes and every line after it, since the lines after it hold the diff that git leaves out of the commit message.

For a merge commit, `sheriff commit-message` counts only the code that differs from its version in every parent of the merge, since each merged commit was checked when it was made.

`sheriff commit-message` runs this check regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-7sk3s553ukzwtbm).
children.reason: The SpecTags on the changed code name the nodes that it implements, so a commit message checked against them records those nodes for whoever reads the history (§s-ef93u6cnbs2sevr).
examples: A commit changes only `src/ui/texts.json`, which the bindings file binds to rule R, and the commit message contains no sid. `sheriff commit-message` refuses the message and names R. The most likely mistake is to read only the SpecTags placed above symbols, which lets the message pass.

children.title: An approved rule whose tests or code lag behind it
children.reason: Unless the tests and code of an approved rule follow its new wording in the same commit, the rule enters the history with tests and code written for its earlier wording (§s-ddd2e96uke4y83j). Only the commit message can state that they need no change, so `sheriff commit-message`, which reads the message, makes the check.
examples: The specification is approved. An earlier commit reworded the approved rule R, so R became a draft. The next commit adds the approval of the new wording and changes R's code but none of its tests. Its message has no trailer naming R. `sheriff commit-message` refuses the commit and says that R's tests lag behind it. The most likely mistake is to compare R's wording with its wording in the commit's parent. That wording is already the new one, so the lag goes unnoticed.

children.reason: Each run of the reviewer is paid for by the user who commits (§s-tnz9zgqx8c629a7), so `sheriff review` runs the reviewer only on a commit that needs one of the reviewer's judgements.
examples: A commit changes only the wording of a draft rule. It changes no code and no comment in the code, its message contains no statement that a rule's implementation needs no change, and it approves no node. So `sheriff review` does not run the reviewer, and the commit passes the review. The most likely mistake is to run the reviewer on every commit, which makes the user who commits pay for a run that has nothing to judge.

todos.by: the agent, after a commit that the reviewer could not review
todos.text: A commit whose change is larger than the reviewer's model can read cannot be reviewed: the runner responds with "Prompt is too long", and the review refuses the commit for that reason. Such a commit passes only after it has been split by hand into smaller commits, each of which keeps the lists of tests in each node consistent with the tests that the commit contains. A rule on how the SpecSheriff tools handle a change of that size, or on how they help to split it, would resolve this problem.

children.title: The judgement on the code that a commit changes
children.reason: A SpecTag shows only which rule a piece of code is meant to implement. Whether the code does only what that rule says, including in the unchanged lines around a change, can be judged only by reading it.
examples: A commit changes one line of the function `close`, whose SpecTag names a rule saying that an account can be closed only when its balance is zero. An unchanged line of the same function also sends the account holder an email. The reviewer is given the whole function and finds that no rule its SpecTag names says anything about the email. `sheriff review` refuses the commit, naming the rule and that line. The most likely mistake is to give the reviewer only the changed line, so that the email goes unnoticed.

decisions.problem: The reviewer was given the commit's change and the nodes it names, and judged the commit as a whole. A tag moved onto a node its symbol does not implement, or a tag naming no node on a symbol carrying the system's logic, passed wherever another named node stated what the code does.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the reviewer is given each changed symbol of the system's code with the tags that bind it, and judges each against the nodes its own tags name. A changed symbol is judged whole, not only its changed lines, since a change anywhere in it is a change of the whole symbol.

children.title: The judgement on a statement that a rule's implementation needs no change
children.text:
`sheriff review` refuses a commit whose message, in the judgement of the independent reviewer (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t), falsely states that a rule's implementation needs no change (§s-nudrdn5xvcg262k). Each finding names the rule. `sheriff review` refuses a commit because of such a finding only where the commit leaves the specification approved (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2). Where the commit leaves it a draft, `sheriff review` disregards such a finding silently.

A commit's message states that a rule's implementation needs no change by means of a trailer (§s-7gab4ptjt2khfr5). The reviewer judges the statement about each rule that such a trailer names, whatever the specification's approval status. For each such rule, `sheriff review` gives the reviewer the tests and the code bound to the rule (§s-6fw72j65jkqrfpf) as the commit leaves them, each in full, with its file, its lines and its SpecTags (§s-8xw4mgvpexyvw5q).
children.reason: Whether a rule's tests and code fit its wording after the commit can be judged only by reading all of them, including those that the commit leaves as they were.
examples: The specification is approved, and a commit corrects a misspelt word in the text of an approved rule without changing its tests or code. Its message ends with the trailer `Implementation-Needs-No-Change: s-…`, which names the rule. The reviewer is given the rule's wording before the commit and after it, its tests and its code, and finds that they fit the new wording. The commit passes. The most likely mistake is to give the reviewer only the code that the commit changes, and here there is none, so that the statement is judged against nothing.

children.title: The judgement on a node of the technical appendix that a commit approves
children.text:
`sheriff review` refuses a commit that approves a node of the technical appendix (§s-tj38pvm38nepaf5) where the independent reviewer (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t) finds that any of the following is true of that node (§s-4p9amamvp2bry7b):
- the node contradicts a rule of the base specification (§s-5x737t9nee4zgaa);
- the node implements a rule of the base specification without refining that rule.

Each finding names the node and the rule of the base specification that the finding concerns. `sheriff review` refuses a commit because of such a finding whatever the specification's approval status (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2).

The reviewer judges each node of the technical appendix for which all of the following hold:
- the commit adds to `specs/_approvals.jsonl` (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb) an entry that approves the node, whoever made the approval;
- the node has an `implements` link (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm) to a rule of the base specification.

In the rule on what the reviewer is given (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q), a top-level section of the base specification means a section whose location (§s-kag2m9tzdnduxdx) consists of the name of a folder, a slash and a single number, such as `base/3` or `requests/2`. For a rule that is in no section (§s-qmmzf9nksfsa3qp), the rules in the same top-level section are the other rules of the same folder of the base specification that are in no section either.
children.reason: An approval names whoever made it only by the email address that git was configured with (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb). An approval that an agent makes on an owner's behalf (§s-t5uw8zfxzhfdg86) therefore looks the same as the owner's own approval. So the reviewer judges every node of the technical appendix that implements a rule of the base specification, whoever approved it.
examples: An agent that is implementing an approved rule saying that an idle session expires adds a node of the technical appendix that sets the idle limit to 30 minutes. The node has an `implements` link to that rule, and the agent approves it on the owner's behalf. Another rule of the same top-level section keeps a session open while a file is being uploaded, which the node's limit breaks during a long upload. `sheriff review` refuses the commit, naming the node and that rule. The most likely mistake is to give the reviewer only the rule that the node implements, so that the contradiction with the rule on uploads goes unnoticed.

children.title: The judgement on a comment that a commit adds or changes
children.reason: A comment that no longer matches its code misleads whoever reads the code next. Only a reader of both the comment and the code can see the mismatch. A comment does not change what the system does, so a problem with a comment warrants a warning, but not a refusal of the commit.
examples: A commit changes only the comment above `roundPrice`, which now says that the function rounds halves up, while the function rounds them to the nearest even number. `sheriff review` reports the reviewer's finding as a warning and lets the commit pass. The most likely mistake is to refuse the commit, as `sheriff review` does for a defect in the code.

children.title: Running the tests before a push
children.text:
The pre-push hook (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw) refuses a push where any test of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc), of the project's own checks (§s-2fau85dfyyeq66m) or of the project's own generators (§s-km4x4s26kv7pjze) fails (§s-aufnqn6t7y2me7a). It runs the tests with the command in `testCommand` in the project-wide settings (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). The tests fail where that command exits with a non-zero status. Where the hook must run the tests and the project-wide settings lack a `testCommand`, it refuses the push and says so.

The pre-push hook runs the tests only where the push creates or updates a ref that points, directly or through a tag, to a commit that meets both of the following conditions:
- the commit leaves the specification approved (§s-qzthyh7yqvfhsa2);
- the project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu), as of that commit, name a push as the moment at which the tests run (§s-x8uzc8z44pwtd3h).

In the commit that a ref points to, the SpecSheriff tools look for `push` in the `TextRule.list` (§s-eferktypcj7njt5) of each rule of `project.json` that has a `refines` link (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm) to the rule on when the tests must pass (§s-x8uzc8z44pwtd3h). They read each rule of `project.json` in its last approved wording as of that commit (§s-a8fn72xa782wvbk). They take each rule's `refines` links from the commit that added the rule's last approval to `specs/_approvals.jsonl`, since an approval does not cover links (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq). Where a member of such a list has the value `push` (§s-5hb9k2e34dgn284), the project's own guidelines name a push as the moment at which the tests run.

Where the push creates or updates a ref and the pre-push hook runs no tests, the hook says so. For each ref that the push creates or updates, it names the reason: in the commit that the ref points to, either the specification is a draft or the project's own guidelines do not name a push as the moment at which the tests run, or both.
children.reason: A project whose own guidelines name a push as the moment at which the tests run relies on the pre-push hook. The hook keeps a change whose tests fail from reaching the project's shared branch (§s-x8uzc8z44pwtd3h).
examples: A project's own guidelines state that the tests run on a shared server before a merge, and none of their rules lists `push`. The specification is approved, and the project-wide settings define a `testCommand`. A developer pushes a branch, and the pre-push hook runs no tests. It says that the project's own guidelines do not name a push as the moment at which the tests run. The most likely mistake is to run the tests because a `testCommand` is set.

decisions.problem: The pre-push hook ran the tests whatever the mode of the specification, while a push in a draft runs none.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-x8uzc8z44pwtd3h: in draft mode the hook runs no test, leaves out the comparison made only for them, and says so.

children.title: The form of a SpecTag
children.reason: Fixed forms, each opening with `@spec`, let the SpecSheriff tools find every SpecTag by its text, in a file in any language. What follows `@spec none` says why the code needs no rule, so that whoever reads the code can tell whether it is technical code (§s-2jcmb9xe9d64t2t).
examples: A function that a web framework calls to register routes, and that holds none of the system's logic, carries `@spec none the web framework requires a function that registers routes`. The most likely mistake is `@spec none helper`, which does not say what the technology requires of the code.

decisions.problem: The tag's rule says a tag stands in the doc comment above the symbol it binds, and nothing checked it: the check read tags by scanning, which finds a tag and can say nothing about what it is attached to. A tag naming a rule and standing over a blank line, or trailing a statement, passed. For the same reason the symbols a node names in its metadata were not graded at all, only the files.
decisions.ruling: Where a tag stands is decided by parsing the file — the parser only, no program and no type checker. A tag binds to the declaration below it where no blank line separates them, and a node that names symbols is held to the ones its tags stand on. A language server was refused for the same job: its answer depends on the state of a running server, and the checks require the same commit to get the same answer every time (§s-jau82aq9juv9zzh).

decisions.problem: The exemption stood at the top of a file, while s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4 now has every declaration carry its own tag.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the exemption stands on the declaration, and on the first of a run of re-exports for the whole run.

decisions.problem: Which declaration a tag stands on was found by one language's parser alone, so the binding could not be held in any other language.
decisions.ruling: The owner: one general parser, with a grammar per language, reads the code; a language is added by describing what counts as a declaration and as a test in it, and TypeScript, JavaScript and Python are described at launch.

decisions.problem: The mark binding a symbol to the node it implements was called a tag, a word git uses for the mark of a release and an ordinary word besides.
decisions.ruling: The owner: it is called SpecTag, written as one word in CamelCase as the method's names are, as RecordType is.

children.title: SpecTags in a file whose language is described
children.text:
In a file whose language is described in the folder `languages/` of the SpecSheriff tools, the SpecTags (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) of a symbol (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4) are lines of the comment directly above the symbol or, where the symbol has decorators, directly above its first decorator. That comment is:
- in TypeScript and JavaScript, the symbol's doc comment;
- in Python, one or more comment lines.

A JSON file is written in JSON Schema if its top-level object's `$schema` is `https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema`. In JSON Schema, whose JSON syntax allows no comments, the symbols of a file are the definitions under the `$defs` of its top-level object. A definition's SpecTags are whole lines of the string in its `$comment`, in place of a comment above the definition (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4). The `$schema` of the top-level object is considered the file's import.

Only the delimiters of the comment may share a SpecTag's line. In JSON Schema, a SpecTag's line is a line of the string in the `$comment`.

In a file of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) other than tests, the code outside every symbol, other than its imports, is bound by the SpecTags in the file's first comment (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4). Those SpecTags bind that code only where the comment comes before any code and is not directly above a symbol. In JSON Schema, those SpecTags are whole lines of the `$comment` of the file's top-level object.

A shebang, a first line that opens with `#!`, may come before the file's first comment. In Python, where a shebang has the form of a comment, the file's first comment is the first comment after the shebang.

In Python, a run of comment lines with no blank line between them is one comment.

In JSON Schema, the code outside every symbol consists of each key of the top-level object, with its value, except `$schema`, `$defs` and `$comment`. So a file of RuntimeChecks (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b) has no code outside its symbols and needs no `$comment` on its top-level object.

Where the first of a run of re-exports, with no blank line between them, carries `@spec none`, that SpecTag also binds each later re-export of the run that carries no SpecTag of its own.

The SpecSheriff tools find the symbol that a SpecTag binds by parsing the file with tree-sitter and the grammar of the file's language. They parse each file on its own, with the parser alone and no type checker.

The description of each language names what is considered a symbol, an import and a test in that language. TypeScript, JavaScript, Python and JSON Schema are described.
children.reason: A SpecTag sits where a reader of the symbol's code already looks. There, a parser, unlike a scan of the text, tells which symbol the SpecTag binds, and gives the same answer for the same file every time.
examples: In TypeScript, `/** @spec s-… */` directly above `export function close()` binds the function and every symbol nested in it. The most likely mistake is a blank line between the comment and the function: the SpecTag is then directly above no symbol and binds nothing.

children.title: SpecTags at the start of a file
children.text:
A file of the system's code (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc) other than tests carries its SpecTags (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) at its start (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4) where all of the following hold:
- the SpecSheriff tools cannot identify the file's symbols, because no description covers its language (§s-33fw3ga4ctd94dq);
- the file's format allows comments (§s-trwczfskj5zmuft).

The SpecTags at the start of a file are on the lines that come before the first of its lines that holds a letter or a digit outside a SpecTag. The file's first line is not counted where it opens with `#!` or `<?`, so that a shebang or a declaration that the format requires to come first, such as an XML declaration, may come before them.

In a file bound by SpecTags at its start, the text that follows `@spec none` runs to the end of its line, excluding any characters at its end that are neither letters nor digits.
children.reason: The lines before a file's content can be identified in any language without parsing. So the SpecTags of a file that the SpecSheriff tools cannot parse are kept there.
examples: A stylesheet starts with `/* @spec s-… */`, followed by the stylesheet's content. An XML file starts with its declaration, `<?xml version="1.0"?>`, followed by `<!-- @spec s-… -->`. The most likely mistake is to put the SpecTag after a licence comment at the start of the file. The words of the licence then come first, and the SpecTag binds nothing.

children.title: The bindings file
children.text:
`sheriff binding` accepts an entry in the bindings file (§s-kgbzk2ph9e6jfb4), `sheriff.bindings.json` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u), only where the entry's path names a file that the commit leaves in the repository (§s-ffkv5qnqvet7bga). At every commit, whether the specification is approved or a draft, it refuses any other entry, naming its path.

The bindings file holds a JSON object. Each key of the object is the path of a file relative to the root of the repository, with forward slashes. The value of each key is the list of the SpecTags (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) of that file, each a string. The SpecSheriff tools refuse a `sheriff.bindings.json` that is not valid JSON or does not hold an object of this form.

The SpecSheriff tools treat a file's format as allowing no comments where the file's name ends in `.json`, or where the file matches the glob patterns that the project's own guidelines (§s-u7tw6m8npxmv5tu) list for such formats.
children.reason: An entry keeps the path it names when its file is moved or renamed. So only a check of every entry against the repository shows that a file has lost its SpecTags.
examples: `src/ui/texts.json` holds the texts that a user interface shows, and the bindings file holds the entry `"src/ui/texts.json": ["@spec s-…"]`. The most likely mistake is to rename the file to `src/ui/labels.json` and leave the entry as it was. `sheriff binding` then refuses the entry, and the renamed file carries no SpecTag.

children.title: How a test declares the rule it is written from
children.text:
A test declares the SpecTag (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) of the rule it is written from (§s-nrjxfvpkq3m8hzm):
- in TypeScript and JavaScript, by starting its name with the SpecTag, as in `test("@spec s-… what it checks", …)`;
- in Python, by a mark on the test, `@pytest.mark.spec("@spec s-…")`;
- in any other language, as the description of that language says (§s-33fw3ga4ctd94dq).

A test declares one SpecTag.

The SpecSheriff tools' plugin for pytest, `pytest-specsheriff`, registers the mark. It puts the test's SpecTag at the start of the name that a run reports for the test.

Where the mark holds anything other than one SpecTag `@spec <sid>`, the plugin stops the run with an error that names the test. Where the mark holds a bare sid (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv), the error also names `sheriff reindex`, which writes the SpecTag.
children.reason: A test run reports each test by its name, so the SpecTag is placed where that report shows it.
examples: In TypeScript, `test("@spec s-… refuses an empty name", …)` declares the SpecTag of the rule it is written from. The most likely mistake is to put the SpecTag only in the name of the `describe` block that holds the tests. That block is not a test, so no test in it declares a SpecTag.

decisions.problem: A test bound to its rule by the opening of its name cannot be written in Python, whose names cannot hold a hyphen.
decisions.ruling: The owner: in Python a test declares its sid by a mark on it; each language's description says how a test declares its sid there.

decisions.problem: A test opened its name with a bare sid, or held one in its mark, while a symbol's SpecTag was `@spec <sid>`.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a test declares `@spec <sid>` where it declared the bare sid, `test("@spec s-… …")` and `@pytest.mark.spec("@spec s-…")`.

children.title: How a commit message states that a rule's implementation needs no change
children.text:
A commit's message states that a rule's implementation needs no change (§s-ddd2e96uke4y83j, §s-nudrdn5xvcg262k) with the trailer `Implementation-Needs-No-Change: <sid>`, in which `<sid>` is the sid of that rule. The message contains one such trailer for each rule about which it makes that statement.

The SpecSheriff tools read the trailers of a message as `git interpret-trailers --parse` reads them. They read a trailer as a statement that a rule's implementation needs no change only where its key is spelt exactly `Implementation-Needs-No-Change` and its value is a single sid.
children.reason: A trailer is the form that git itself provides for a statement about a commit, so git and other tools read it without parsing the message's prose.
examples: A commit changes the text of an approved rule only to correct a misspelt word. Its message ends with the line `Implementation-Needs-No-Change: s-…`, which names the rule. children.title: Which runner runs the reviewer
children.text:
`sheriff review` hands everything that the independent reviewer (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t) is given (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q) to a runner. A runner is an agent's CLI that `sheriff review` starts for each review (§s-avvnasjhsfkgajh). A runner is either `claude` (§s-3wh8uhgn9jr2k74) or `codex` (§s-u2n5hwwqkb6zk4z).

`sheriff review` runs the runner that `review.runner` in `sheriff.config.json` names (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). The default of `review.runner` is the runner of the SpecSheriff plugin whose tools run `sheriff review`. The build of each SpecSheriff plugin writes the file `agent` into the folder of the plugin's SpecSheriff tools. That file names the plugin's runner:
- `claude` for the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5);
- `codex` for the plugin for Codex CLI (§s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4).

SpecSheriff tools that have no file `agent` use `claude`.

The project-wide settings of the reviewer in `sheriff.config.json` are `review.runner` and `review.minutes`. `review.minutes` sets the time limit of a run of the reviewer (§s-wgedv32rdaqca9k).
children.reason: A user with one agent has no other agent to run, so the default runner is that of the plugin that the user has installed. A project that wants one runner for everyone names it in `review.runner`.

children.title: The reviewer's verdict
children.text:
`sheriff review` refuses a commit for which the reviewer must make a judgement other than the one on comments (§s-vp24dqydygztqbt) unless the runner (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u) gives a verdict that `sheriff review` can read (§s-94k7b6r5kf65udf). Where the commit needs only the judgement on comments (§s-7vpsdsy8dpqdy6r), `sheriff review` instead issues a warning that says why it could not read a verdict.

`sheriff review` gives the runner's CLI the schema of the verdict. The runner's CLI answers with a JSON object that conforms to that schema. The verdict passes or refuses the commit. It lists its findings. Each finding names the sids of the nodes that it concerns and the problem. A finding that concerns code also names the file and, where the problem lies on a particular line, that line. Each finding also names the judgement that it belongs to (§s-vp24dqydygztqbt).

`sheriff review` reads a verdict only from an answer that conforms to the schema of the verdict and that does one of the following:
- passes the commit and lists only findings that belong to the judgement on comments (§s-7vpsdsy8dpqdy6r), if it lists any;
- refuses the commit and lists at least one finding that belongs to a judgement other than the one on comments.
children.reason: A verdict whose meaning `sheriff review` had to guess, such as a verdict that passes the commit and lists a finding on code, would let `sheriff review` decide the outcome of the commit in place of the independent reviewer (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t).
examples: The runner answers with a verdict that passes the commit and lists one finding on code. That answer is not a verdict that `sheriff review` can read, so `sheriff review` refuses the commit. The most likely mistake is to pass the commit and drop the finding, which means deciding for the reviewer what it meant.

decisions.problem: The rewrite of the tools lost what kept the session that wrote the code away from the runner. Every variable of the environment reached the runner, among them those an agent sets for its session and git's, which the hooks point at the repository. On Windows the CLI ran through a shell, and the time limit ended the shell while the CLI went on. Only the runner `codex` held its answer to the schema of the verdict, and an answer passing the commit with findings passed it.
decisions.ruling: The runner's environment holds only the variables a list allows, the exact names settled when the code is written, after trial runs of both runners. The CLI is started as a program, never through a shell. Every runner is given the schema of the verdict. An answer that contradicts itself is read as one that cannot be read.

children.title: How a runner is started
children.reason: Anything that reaches the runner from the session that made the change, such as the user's memory or the repository through git's variables, lets it judge by more than the rules (§s-nyh9yk22ba6g77q). A shell between `sheriff review` and the runner would read the runner's arguments, such as the schema of the verdict, according to its own syntax and could change them.
examples: Claude Code sets `CLAUDECODE` for its session, and git sets `GIT_DIR` to the repository for each hook it runs. Neither variable is in the list, so neither reaches the runner. The runner therefore cannot read the repository through `GIT_DIR` from its empty working directory. The most likely mistake is to remove only the variables on a list of known ones, which fails to remove each variable that a new release of an agent adds.

children.title: The settings of each runner
children.text:
`sheriff review` reads the settings of each runner (§s-xr5xxa9cxf2mq5u) from the git configuration of the user who commits:
- `specsheriff.review.claudeModel`, `specsheriff.review.claudeFallbackModel` and `specsheriff.review.claudeEffort`, for the runner `claude` (§s-3wh8uhgn9jr2k74);
- `specsheriff.review.codexModel` and `specsheriff.review.codexEffort`, for the runner `codex` (§s-u2n5hwwqkb6zk4z).

`sheriff review` takes the model and the reasoning effort only from these settings and their defaults. Where a setting is empty, `sheriff review` leaves the choice of the setting's value to the runner's CLI. An empty `specsheriff.review.codexModel`, for example, means the model that Codex chooses for the signed-in account.

A setting that the user's git configuration holds, empty or not, counts as confirmed. The agent's hooks (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw) and the skills of each SpecSheriff plugin (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5, §s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4) ask only for a setting that this configuration lacks. They write a setting into a user's git configuration only with the value that this user gives in reply. Where the user answers with the default, they write it like any other value.

The defaults are:
- for the runner `claude`, the model `opus` at the reasoning effort `high`, with `sonnet` as the fallback model;
- for the runner `codex`, the model that Codex chooses, at the reasoning effort `high`.

Where the user's git configuration lacks a setting of the runner in use, `sheriff review` takes that setting's default. In every review (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t) that runs with a default setting, `sheriff review` names each setting whose default it took, and says how the user confirms that setting.
children.reason: A run of the reviewer (§s-m4h279nbaqkpa3t) is paid for by the user who commits, from their own account. That user alone therefore controls the models and the reasoning efforts that the reviewer runs with.
examples: A user confirms `specsheriff.review.claudeModel` once with `git config --global`. From then on, every review made with the runner `claude` on that machine runs with that model, including after the plugin is updated, or removed and installed again. The most likely mistake is to keep the model in `sheriff.config.json`, which every clone shares, so that everyone who commits pays for one person's choice.

decisions.problem: The reviewer ran at the models the tools or the project's settings chose, the same for every clone, though each run is paid for by the user who commits; and at the effort Codex takes by default its verdicts on one and the same change differed from run to run: with Codex CLI 0.166.0, a ChatGPT sign-in and gpt-6-luna, a function no named rule states passed in one run of four at the default effort and in three of three at medium, and was refused in three of three at high and at max.
decisions.ruling: The owner: no choice that costs a user tokens is made without their consent. The skills work at the model and the effort the user has chosen in their session; every run outside it, now the reviewer's, at the model and the effort the user has confirmed on their machine, offered first at defaults, one model for each agent at an effort set by the task: opus at high falling back to sonnet, since a model above opus is not worth its cost to the user here and Anthropic itself now recommends opus over fable, and the model Codex chooses at high. Each user confirms on their own machine; where they have not, the defaults run with a notice at every commit.

children.text: How the SpecSheriff tools record the approval of a node (§s-67vekyup7y8smap) and the withdrawal of that approval (§s-fpq35tf3pehgk64), and how they tell whether an approval is in force.

children.title: How an approval is recorded
children.reason: A node's approval decides whether its code may change, so the SpecSheriff tools take the approval from a record that no edit to the node changes and that keeps every approval and every withdrawal, each with the email address of whoever made it.
examples: Rule R was approved with the wording whose fingerprint is F1, then reworded and approved with the fingerprint F2. Someone then withdrew R's approval, which appended a withdrawal for F1 and then one for F2. No approval of any of R's wordings is in force, so R is a draft, and R's last approval is the line that approved F2. The most likely mistake is to treat R as approved because a line in the file approves its current wording, although a later line withdraws that approval.

decisions.problem: Confirmations were kept in one person's files outside the repository, guarded by that person's hooks, so nobody else could check a status and a lost file would have emptied every status.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a confirmation is kept with the specification, names who gave it and is accepted only under that owner's signature.

decisions.problem: The line withdrawing a confirmation named whoever withdrew it as its owner, though anyone may withdraw one.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-5ah25f6gy99panq: anyone may withdraw an approval, and the line that records the withdrawal names whoever withdraws the approval in its `by` field.

decisions.problem: The owner renamed a node's id to location, its rationale to reason and the kind record to RecordType, while every project's files and confirmations hold the old names.
decisions.ruling: A technical consequence in the owner's name: the reason keeps its old label in the fingerprint, so no confirmation is lost.

decisions.problem: `sheriff reindex` rewrites a field's own empty list, which an earlier release wrote for a field of type `one of`, into the source the domains add. This changed the fingerprint, so every RecordType approved with such a field would have lost its approval at the first reindex after an upgrade.
decisions.ruling: The owner: such a field stands in the fingerprint's string as earlier releases wrote it, as the reason stands under its earlier name.

decisions.problem: The act was called confirm, recorded under one owner in `_confirmations.jsonl`.
decisions.ruling: The owner: the act is approve, `sheriff approve`, recorded in `_approvals.jsonl` naming who approved; no alias kept.

decisions.problem: A withdrawal took back only the latest approval of the node, so the approval of an earlier wording still stood: an edit restoring that wording could write the status back to approved with no owner approving it after the withdrawal, the rule that approves the specification included.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a withdrawal takes back the approval of each wording of the node for which one stands, whether the node holds that wording or not, one line per wording.

decisions.problem: The reason held that the lines two branches append merge without a conflict, while git reported one, and a merge can set lines in another order than the one they were written in.
decisions.ruling: In line with the owner's ruling on §s-7unxytshhc4md54: the lines merge without a conflict when git merges the approvals by union, and the latest line is the one that comes last in the file.

children.title: The fingerprint of a node's wording
children.reason: An approval records a wording by its fingerprint, so that a change to that wording leaves the node without an approval in force, and no other change to the node does (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq). A string built the same way everywhere gives every machine and every release the same fingerprint for the same wording.
examples: A rule is approved, and an edit adds an example to it. The rule's fingerprint changes, so no approval of its new wording is in force, and `sheriff reindex` makes the rule a draft. A later edit adds a link to the rule and moves it to another section, and its fingerprint stays the same. The most likely mistake is to leave the examples out of the object, so that the rule stays approved with an example that no owner has read.

Each row of a `TableRule` holds a rule and text that says what a failure of that rule costs. The cost in one row changes from `refused` to `reported`. The fingerprint of the rule in that row changes, since the text cells of its row are part of its wording, and the fingerprint of the `TableRule` changes too. The most likely mistake is to build the object for the rule from its own properties alone, so that the rule stays approved with a cost that no owner has approved.

children.title: Approving a node
children.text:
`sheriff approve <sid>...` approves each node that it names (§s-67vekyup7y8smap). For each such node, it appends to `specs/_approvals.jsonl` an approval (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb) of the node's current wording (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq). The approval holds the email address of whoever runs the command.

`sheriff approve` then sets the status of each node that it names to `approved`. Where an approval of a node's current wording is already in force, `sheriff approve` appends nothing for that node and only sets the node's status.

Where a node that `sheriff approve` names is a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6), the command also approves each node in the table's cells, in the same way as it approves a node that it names. It appends these approvals after that of the `TableRule`, in the order of the table's rows and, within a row, in the order of its columns.

`sheriff approve` refuses each of the following:
- a sid that names no node in the files that the repository keeps, such as the sid of a node of the SpecSheriff guidelines or of a chosen extension (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) in a project other than SpecSheriff itself, since such a project takes those nodes from the plugin (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab);
- a section or, where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), the header of a domain (§s-yccuyqbypzzx2gu), since `sheriff reindex` derives the approval status of either from other nodes (§s-ztseyetus7np6br);
- a node whose owners do not include whoever runs the command (§s-6sk8uet75dmq5qz).

Each refusal names the sid concerned. The refusal of a node whose owners do not include whoever runs the command also names the node's owners.

Where `sheriff approve` refuses any sid named in the run, it records none of the run's approvals and changes no node's status. Where git's configuration sets no email address, `sheriff approve` refuses to run.

After it records the approvals, `sheriff approve` runs `sheriff reindex` (§s-ztseyetus7np6br).
children.reason: Recording every approval through one command lets the SpecSheriff tools check, before an approval is recorded, that whoever gives it is an owner of the node (§s-67vekyup7y8smap).
examples: A rule of a project's base specification is a `TableRule`, each row of which holds one state of a request as a node. An owner adds two rows, whose nodes are drafts, and runs `sheriff approve` with the table's sid. `sheriff approve` appends an approval of the table's new wording and one approval of the node in each new row. The most likely mistake is to approve only the table, so that the nodes of the new rows stay drafts.

children.title: Withdrawing the approval of a node
children.text:
`sheriff approve --withdraw <sid>...` withdraws the approval of each node that it names (§s-fpq35tf3pehgk64). For each approval of a wording (§s-5ah25f6gy99panq) of such a node, if that approval is in force, whether or not the node still holds that wording, the command appends to `specs/_approvals.jsonl` a line that withdraws that approval (§s-v4qus7raqnwzneb). Each such line holds the email address of whoever runs the command. The command appends these lines in the order in which the first line for each such wording appears in the file.

`sheriff approve --withdraw` then sets the status of each node that it names to `draft`. Where no approval of any wording of a node is in force, `sheriff approve --withdraw` appends nothing for that node and only sets the node's status.

Where a node that `sheriff approve --withdraw` names is a `TableRule` (§s-5fewsp22mmdz7y6), the command withdraws only the approvals of the table's own wordings. To withdraw the approval of a node in a cell of the table, whoever runs the command names that node.

`sheriff approve --withdraw` records a withdrawal by whoever runs it, whether or not they are among the node's owners. It refuses each of the following:
- a sid that names no node in the files that the repository keeps, such as the sid of a node of the SpecSheriff guidelines or of a chosen extension (§s-9ttvcwpqkehm58g) in a project other than SpecSheriff itself, since such a project takes those nodes from the plugin (§s-bsya3febm6u64ab);
- a section or, where the project has chosen the Domains extension (§s-tdm3rwsppnuh6dm), the header of a domain (§s-yccuyqbypzzx2gu), since `sheriff reindex` derives the approval status of either from other nodes (§s-ztseyetus7np6br).

Each refusal names the sid concerned. Where `sheriff approve --withdraw` refuses any sid named in the run, it records none of the run's withdrawals and changes no node's status. Where git's configuration sets no email address, `sheriff approve --withdraw` refuses to run.

After it records the withdrawals, `sheriff approve --withdraw` runs `sheriff reindex` (§s-ztseyetus7np6br).
children.reason: A withdrawal takes back the approval of the node, not only that of the wording that the node holds now (§s-fpq35tf3pehgk64). An approval left in force for an earlier wording would let an edit that restores that wording make the node approved again without any owner approving it.
examples: Rule R was approved, reworded and approved again, so an approval of each of its wordings is in force. A developer who is not an owner of R finds that R is wrong and runs `sheriff approve --withdraw` with R's sid. The command appends a withdrawal for each of those wordings, and R becomes a draft. The most likely mistake is to withdraw only the approval of R's current wording, so that an edit that restores R's earlier wording makes R approved again.

children.title: A git hook runs the SpecSheriff tools that a plugin keeps on the machine
children.text:
When a session starts, the plugin for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5) copies the SpecSheriff tools that it holds into its data directory, unless its data directory already holds a copy of the same release. The data directory is `<plugins>/data/specsheriff-specsheriff-marketplace/`. `<plugins>` is `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_CACHE_DIR` where that variable is set, and `~/.claude/plugins` otherwise.

The plugin for Codex CLI (§s-2pdy9gw2jrjvfb4) keeps its SpecSheriff tools only in its directory in Codex's cache, `<Codex home>/plugins/cache/specsheriff-marketplace/specsheriff/<version>/tools/`. `<Codex home>` is `CODEX_HOME` where that variable is set, and `~/.codex` otherwise.

`~` is the user's home directory, which on Windows is the user's profile directory.

Each git hook that `sheriff init` writes (§s-7unxytshhc4md54) does the following:
- it looks for the SpecSheriff tools of each plugin;
- where the SpecSheriff tools can run, it calls the script for that hook in their `hooks/`;
- where the SpecSheriff tools cannot run, it runs the project's own tools for that hook (§s-n4m5zvh96yb299p).

Where the hook finds the SpecSheriff tools of both plugins, it takes those whose `release` file begins with the higher version, the versions being compared as semantic versions. Where their versions are equal, it takes either set.

The script for the hook runs what the list of the hooks specifies for that hook (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), including the project's own tools for that hook.

The SpecSheriff tools cannot run where the hook finds the tools of neither plugin, or where Node.js is missing or older than the version that the `engines` field of their `package.json` names. In either case, the hook lets the commit or the push through unless one of the project's own tools fails (§s-pcnyfp7gev7syax). The pre-commit and pre-push hooks then say that the SpecSheriff tools ran no check, and why: either no plugin's SpecSheriff tools are on the machine, or Node.js is missing or older than that version, which the hooks name.

The hook that runs when a session starts (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw) names each of the following hooks that holds what an earlier release of `sheriff init` wrote:
- each git hook in `.githooks/`;
- each of the agent's hooks for Codex in `.codex/hooks.json`.

For each such hook, it says that running `sheriff init` again replaces that hook.
children.reason: A git hook written once into a project finds the SpecSheriff tools wherever a machine keeps them and whichever plugin they come from, so that the checks keep up with each release of the plugin without any change to the project. Where those tools cannot run, the project's own tools keep guarding the commit and the push, as the rule on the order of tools and checks requires (§s-pcnyfp7gev7syax).
examples: A user has both plugins: the plugin for Claude Code at release 0.7.0 and the plugin for Codex CLI at release 0.6.0. Each git hook runs the SpecSheriff tools of 0.7.0 from the data directory of the plugin for Claude Code, even when the commit is made from Codex. The most likely mistake is to take the tools of the agent that is running, so that a commit made from Codex is checked by the earlier release.

children.title: The project's own tools in a git hook
children.text:
A project's own tools for a git hook are the files directly in `.githooks/<hook>.d/` whose first line names their interpreter. Each git hook that `sheriff init` writes (§s-7unxytshhc4md54) runs only those files, and names any other file in that directory.

A first line names an interpreter where it starts with `#!`, followed by a path and at most one argument. A carriage return that ends the line is ignored.

Where the hook runs the SpecSheriff tools (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p), it runs the project's own tools at the points set by the order of that hook's steps (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw, §s-pcnyfp7gev7syax):
- first, those that the project's own guidelines list as tools that rewrite files (§s-t9j29hppag2nren), in the order of that list;
- then, the other tools, in the byte order of their names.

Where a path in the project's list of tools that rewrite files points into the hook's own folder, `.githooks/<hook>.d/`, and the hook runs nothing for that path, the hook names the path.

Where the SpecSheriff tools cannot run (§s-4mej6ccn7xu3d3p), the hook runs all of the project's own tools for that hook in the byte order of their names.

The hook runs each of the project's own tools as follows:
- from the root of the working tree, with the interpreter that the tool's first line names, in the environment that git gives the hook, so that the tool reads the working tree and git's index;
- with the arguments that git hands the hook, and with a copy of the standard input that git hands the hook.

Each of the project's own tools runs even if another of them has failed. The hook fails where one of them exits with a code other than zero.

Where the hook runs the SpecSheriff tools, it also refuses the commit or the push if one of the project's own tools that run after the tools that rewrite files does any of the following, regardless of whether the specification is approved or a draft (§s-yn5tdx2bp4f5rq7):
- adds, changes or removes a file of the working tree, other than a file that git ignores;
- changes what is staged;
- changes the commit message.

The hook names each tool that makes it fail, and each file that such a tool added, changed or removed.

A project's own tools for a git hook are among the repository's own tools (§s-hheus6f395ynqvc).
children.reason: A project's own tools check what the checks of the SpecSheriff tools do not check, for example by scanning for secrets, so they run on every machine, whether or not the SpecSheriff tools can run there. They run at the points that the rule on the order of tools and checks sets (§s-pcnyfp7gev7syax), so that none of them changes what a check has read. A tool is recognised by its first line rather than by the executable bit, since a file committed from a system without that bit loses it.
examples: `.githooks/pre-commit.d/` holds `scan` and `tidy`, and the project's own guidelines list `pre-commit.d/tidy` as a tool that rewrites files. On a commit, `tidy` runs first and stages the files that it rewrites. `scan` runs after `sheriff types`, and the hook refuses the commit where `scan` changes any file that git does not ignore. The most likely mistake is to run both in the byte order of their names, so that `scan` reads the files before `tidy` has rewritten them.

decisions.problem: The project's own tools needed a way to be registered that a hook can read even where no SpecSheriff tools are on the machine.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a project registers its own tools for a hook by placing them in .githooks/<hook>.d/, which the hook reads at every run, rather than by a list in sheriff.config.json, which a hook without the SpecSheriff tools could not read; sheriff init neither knows nor registers them.

children.title: The plugin for Claude Code
children.reason: An agent can use a skill only where the skill is installed. Claude Code installs, updates and enables a plugin that a project declares. So the plugin brings the skills, the SpecSheriff guidelines with their extensions and the SpecSheriff tools, all from the same release, to the agent in every clone. The project itself keeps only the declaration of the plugin and the calls to the plugin's tools.
examples: A project chooses the RecordType extension. On every machine where Claude Code has updated the plugin to a release that delivers that extension, the SpecSheriff tools find the extension at `guidelines/extensions/recordtype.json` in their own folder. The most likely mistake is to keep a copy of the extension in `specs/_guidelines/extensions/`, which `sheriff validate` refuses (§s-6bmnsbskg6en4nf).

decisions.ruling: The owner: the main channel is a plugin of skills for the agents, distributed through a marketplace; the plugin is made for Claude Code now and for Codex CLI next, and Gemini CLI is being studied.

decisions.ruling: The owner: the plugin's skills and the agent's hooks run them from the tools the plugin carries, by the directory Claude Code writes in for the installed release.

The plugin for Claude Code declares the settings of the runner claude as its options, each naming its default and taking no default value; spec-init offers the defaults of any setting still lacking that was never asked for; the skills set no model and no effort.

decisions.ruling: The owner: the skills keep their names. Claude Code shows a plugin's skill under the plugin's name, as specsheriff:spec-review, and loads a user's skill of the same name beside it, so the plugin's name already keeps them distinct. A call by hand keeps that name either way, so a shorter skill name would save almost nothing, and the agent mostly takes the skills up by their descriptions. The name spec-review says what the skill works on, where ss-review has to be decoded. And ss reads first as the abbreviation of the Nazi SS, besides being a standard Linux command.

children.title: The plugin for Codex CLI
children.text:
The plugin for Codex CLI, `specsheriff`, holds the skills of the SpecSheriff plugins (§s-kq6wmdud9c7j2k9). It holds the SpecSheriff tools, with the files common to every project (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u), and the scripts of the agent's hooks (§s-477gtdrkw34dzxw), as the plugin for Claude Code does (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5).

The agent's hooks for Codex are in the project, not in the plugin (§s-n76wt2bkqdmh78x). They call the scripts that the plugin holds.

The marketplace `specsheriff-marketplace` lists the plugin by the relative path of its directory, in `.agents/plugins/marketplace.json` at the root of the repository where the SpecSheriff guidelines are written, which also holds the marketplace for Claude Code (§s-zh2vcr3xjumppg5).

The practitioner's guide, the plugin's `README.md`, gives the commands that install the plugin on a machine:
- `codex plugin marketplace add non4me/SpecSheriff@release`;
- `codex plugin add specsheriff@specsheriff-marketplace`.

The plugin's skills run `sheriff` from the SpecSheriff tools in the plugin, as `node <plugin>/tools/dist/cli.js`. A skill derives `<plugin>` from the path of its `SKILL.md`, `<plugin>/skills/<skill>/SKILL.md`.
children.reason: An agent can use a skill only where the skill is installed. Codex installs a plugin only for the user who adds it, so each user has to install the plugin for Codex CLI. Each release of that plugin holds the same skills and SpecSheriff tools as the release of the plugin for Claude Code that has the same version, so that a project's users follow the same procedures and are held to the same checks whichever agent each runs.

children.title: The skill `spec-settings`
children.text:
`spec-settings` shows in the chat the settings that only an owner of the specification changes, as `sheriff settings` prints them (§s-chsfpkgpmfk4fft). It then asks the user to choose one of the following ways to change them:
- `sheriff settings` in a separate terminal window, which the skill offers only where it can open such a window on the graphical desktop of the machine that runs the session;
- questions in the chat.

Where the user chooses questions in the chat, the skill runs `sheriff settings` with the arguments for each change that the user asks for. Where the user chooses the terminal window, the skill reports, once the window closes, how the settings that `sheriff settings` prints differ from those that it showed before.
children.reason: These settings are changed only with `sheriff settings`, which records a change only where an owner makes it (§s-chsfpkgpmfk4fft). `sheriff settings` in a terminal window needs a desktop that the owner can see, which an owner who works remotely does not have, so the skill also offers the chat.
examples: An owner works from a browser through Remote Control and asks the agent to choose the Views extension. `spec-settings` offers a separate terminal window or questions in the chat, and the owner chooses the chat. The skill runs `sheriff settings extension views on`. The most likely mistake is to open the window without asking, on a desktop that the owner cannot see.

decisions.problem: How an owner who works on a machine whose screen they cannot see, for example through Remote Control, changes the settings that only an owner changes. A skill cannot tell whether the user sees the desktop of the machine that runs the session.
decisions.ruling: The owner ruled that the skill offers both `sheriff settings` in a separate terminal window on that machine and questions in the chat, and leaves the choice to the user. The window is offered first, since the owner named running the program in a terminal as the main way ("да делаем").

children.title: The agent's hooks for Codex CLI
children.reason: The agent's hooks for Codex hold an agent working in Codex to the same checks, before and after each edit, as an agent in Claude Code. Codex's public plugin directory admits no plugin that contains hooks, so the agent's hooks for Codex are in the project. Codex runs a project's hook only after its user has trusted the hook as it is written. So a hook that only finds the plugin and calls its scripts does not have to be trusted again when a release of the plugin changes what the scripts do.
examples: A patch adds `src/new.ts` and changes `specs/_approvals.jsonl`. `sheriff guard` refuses the patch, and `hooks/guard.sh` writes the denial as JSON with the refusal in `permissionDecisionReason`, so Codex applies no part of the patch. The most likely mistake is to write the refusal to standard output as plain text, which Codex ignores before a tool call, so that the patch is applied.

children.title: Where the types and RuntimeChecks generated from the RecordTypes are written
children.text:
Where the project has chosen the RecordType extension (§s-hzuzn8hbq6q9q4s), `sheriff types` (§s-a8fn72xa782wvbk) writes the types and the RuntimeChecks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9) that it generates from the RecordTypes (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3) only into the files that the technical appendix (§s-tj38pvm38nepaf5) lists for them.

The list of those files is the `TextRule.list` (§s-eferktypcj7njt5) of a rule in the section of the technical appendix on the stack (§s-vj7ercem526zd6v), `specs/tech/stack.json` (§s-zefk589ykh37b8u). That rule is the one that has both a `TextRule.list` and an `implements` link to the rule on generating the types and the RuntimeChecks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9). Each member of the list is the path of a file relative to the root of the repository.

`sheriff types` reads the list in that rule's last approved wording (§s-a8fn72xa782wvbk). A rule that has never been approved lists no file. `sheriff types` reads the rule's `implements` links from the same place as the SpecSheriff tools read the `refines` links of a rule of the project's own guidelines (§s-t9j29hppag2nren): from the commit that added the rule's last approval or, until that commit is made, from the files of the specification.

The extension of a listed file's name determines what `sheriff types` writes into the file:
- `.ts`: the types in TypeScript;
- `.py`: the types in Python;
- `.json`: the RuntimeChecks in JSON Schema 2020-12.

The check of generated copies (§s-dbk2vyeg8z5jxna) refuses a list that names a file whose name has any other extension, as it refuses everything else that keeps `sheriff types` from writing any file at all.
children.reason: Where the generated code goes is a choice that concerns the whole system, so the technical appendix describes it in its section on the stack (§s-mm2de262g3jkapu).
examples: The rule in the section on the stack lists `src/generated/records.ts` and `src/generated/records.schema.json`. `sheriff types` writes the types of the RecordTypes into the first file and their RuntimeChecks into the second. A team member adds `worker/records.py` to the list, so the rule becomes a draft. Until the new wording is approved, `sheriff types` writes nothing into `worker/records.py`. The most likely mistake is to take the list from the draft wording.

children.title: What is generated from a RecordType
children.text:
From the last approved wording of each RecordType (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3, §s-a8fn72xa782wvbk), `sheriff types` writes a type into each file of types and a definition into each file of RuntimeChecks (§s-pvzms7d8kxb8dk2). It takes the RecordTypes in the code-point order of their files' paths and, within a file, in the order in which the computation of locations visits them (§s-ygg5kpcxgzq3m7w).

The name of a RecordType's type and of its definition is the RecordType's title, with the first letter of each word changed to uppercase and the spaces removed.

Each type has the SpecTag `@spec <sid>` (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) with the sid of its RecordType (§s-ktfstpv8rurznrp), in the comment directly above it (§s-33fw3ga4ctd94dq): `/** @spec <sid> */` in TypeScript and `# @spec <sid>` in Python. Each definition has that SpecTag as the first line of its `$comment`, before any text of the `$comment` of the RecordType's `schema`. Each definition has the sid of its RecordType as its `$anchor`, by which a `$ref` in another definition points to it (§s-4npdup7mjkva69y).

A file of RuntimeChecks holds one JSON Schema document, whose `$schema` is `https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema` and whose `$defs` holds each definition under its name.

The fields of a type and of a definition are, first, the fields of each RecordType that the type's RecordType reaches through `refines` links (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm). Its own fields, which its `schema` declares (§s-6eb92ddch7shuvu), follow them. The SpecSheriff tools follow the `refines` links of a RecordType in the order in which it lists them. For each link, they first take the RecordTypes that the linked RecordType reaches in this way, and then the linked RecordType itself. They take each RecordType only the first time that they reach it.

Each field keeps its name and the place where it first appears. Where several of these RecordTypes declare a field with the same name, the field's schema in a definition is an `allOf` that holds their schemas in the order in which they are taken. In a type, the field has the type that the last of these schemas gives (§s-4npdup7mjkva69y). A field is guaranteed (§s-adhmw4gw6y82f44) where the `required` of the `schema` of any of these RecordTypes lists it. In a type, a guaranteed field is required, and any other field is optional.

A definition is built from the RecordType's own `schema`. In the definition, `properties` holds these fields and `required` lists the guaranteed ones. Each field's schema in it is changed only as the node on the type given by a field's schema says (§s-4npdup7mjkva69y). Where a RecordType has RecordType variants (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j), the node on such a RecordType (§s-nk8td3ez58gahc4) says what `sheriff types` generates for it and for each of its variants in place of, or in addition to, what this node says.

In TypeScript, a type is written `export type <name> = {...}`, with `?` after the name of each optional field.

In Python:
- a type is written `<name> = TypedDict("<name>", {...})`;
- each name that a type uses from `typing` is imported from `typing`;
- a reference to another type is written as a string;
- an optional field is marked `NotRequired`.

`sheriff types` cannot generate the name of a type or of a definition in any of these cases (§s-dbk2vyeg8z5jxna):
- the name is not an identifier in the language of its file;
- the file already uses the name, including the names that the file imports and those that its language reserves;
- a `$ref` names a sid that no RecordType has, so the type that the `$ref` refers to has no name.
children.reason: Generated in one fixed way, the types and the definitions come out the same on every run and on every machine. The check of generated copies relies on that (§s-dbk2vyeg8z5jxna). Named after its RecordType and bound to it by a SpecTag that `sheriff types` writes, each type leads its reader back to the RecordType that it comes from.
examples: A fragment of a format named `address` declares the fields `city` and `street`. The RecordType `user` refines `address` and declares `name` and `street`, with a narrower schema for `street`. The type `User` holds `city`, then `street` with the type that `user` gives it, and then `name`. The definition `User` checks `street` against the schemas of both RecordTypes. The most likely mistake is to write `street` twice in the type, once for each RecordType, which TypeScript refuses to compile.

children.title: A RecordType that its variants refine
children.text:
For a RecordType (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3) that has RecordType variants (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j), `sheriff types` writes a definition and a type that also describe the fields of each variant. In every other respect, it writes them as it writes those of any RecordType (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b).

The variants of such a RecordType are the RecordType variants whose RecordType it is, as the check of RecordType variants determines (§s-c2r9jndrjbtbsv6). `sheriff types` takes each variant in its last approved wording (§s-a8fn72xa782wvbk), in the order in which it takes the RecordTypes. It leaves out a variant that has never been approved. Where it leaves out every variant of a RecordType, it writes the RecordType's definition and type as it writes those of any RecordType.

In a file of RuntimeChecks (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9), the RecordType's definition also holds an `if` and `then` pair for each of its variants, at the end of its `allOf`:
- `if` is `{"properties": {<field>: {"const": <value>}, …}, "required": [<field>, …]}`, with each field and value that the variant's `answersTo` (§s-c2r9jndrjbtbsv6) names;
- `then` is `{"$ref": "#<sid>"}`, with the sid of the variant, so that it points to the variant's definition.

Where the RecordType's `schema` holds no `allOf`, the definition holds an `allOf` with only these pairs.

A variant's definition is written as the definition of any RecordType, except that it holds only the fields that the variant adds to its RecordType. These are the fields that the variant declares and the fields of each RecordType that it reaches through `refines` links (§s-sn6au3vcr9uy5pm), other than its RecordType and the RecordTypes that its RecordType reaches.

In a file of types, the RecordType's type is the union of the following members, each a type of its own:
- for each variant, the variant's type;
- where a combination of values of the fields that select a variant has no variant, a type for the combinations that have no variant; its name is the name of the RecordType's type followed by `Other`.

The type of a variant is written as the type of any RecordType (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b), except that each field that selects a variant is required in it and takes only the value that the variant's `answersTo` (§s-c2r9jndrjbtbsv6) names.

The type for the combinations that have no variant is written right after the union. It holds the RecordType's fields. Where one field selects a variant, that field takes only the values to which no variant corresponds. Where several fields select a variant, each of them takes all its values.

The union is written `export type <name> = <member> | …` in TypeScript and `<name> = Union["<member>", …]` in Python. The union has the SpecTag (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) of the RecordType. Each member has the SpecTag of the RecordType that it comes from: a variant's type has the SpecTag of the variant, and the type for the combinations that have no variant has the SpecTag of the RecordType. A variant's definition has the SpecTag of the variant as the first line of its `$comment`, as the definition of any RecordType does (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b).

The values of a field that selects a variant are those that the SpecSheriff tools collect for it (§s-5nf87c3e3jg9v7c).
children.reason: A data record holds the fields of its RecordType together with those of the RecordType variant that its values select (§s-z3dnru6qqdf9m6j). The types and RuntimeChecks generated from the RecordType describe such a data record with the construct that each language provides for fields that depend on the value of another field.
examples: The RecordType `notification` names `channel` in its `chosenBy`, and the values of `channel` are `email`, `sms` and `app`. Its variants, titled “notification by email” and “notification by SMS”, correspond to `email` and `sms`; the first declares the guaranteed field `address`, and the second the guaranteed field `phone`. Its definition holds an `if` and `then` pair for each of them, and its type `Notification` is the union of `NotificationByEmail`, `NotificationBySMS` and `NotificationOther`, in which `channel` takes only `app`. The most likely mistake is to let `channel` take every value in `NotificationOther`, so a data record whose `channel` is `email` and that has no `address` is accepted by the type.

children.title: The type that the schema of a field gives
children.text:
Within a RecordType's `schema` (§s-7vm323mhry2enx3, §s-6eb92ddch7shuvu), the schema of each field gives, in TypeScript and in Python, the type that the table below names. The last column of the table names the neutral type that an earlier release of the SpecSheriff tools wrote in place of each schema (§s-gb8s9657a65hqmv).

| Field's schema | TypeScript | Python | Neutral type that an earlier release wrote |
|---|---|---|---|
| `{"$ref": "#<sid>"}` | the name of the type of the RecordType that has that sid | that name, as a string | record |
| `{"identifierOf": "<sid>"}` | what the field at the end of the field's chain of identifiers gives (§s-3anv9qcmx8pwp2w) | what that field gives | identifier of |
| `{"const": <its value>}` | the literal of its value | `Literal[<its value>]` | — |
| `{"enum": [<its values>]}` | the union of its values as literals | `Literal[<its values>]` | one of, with a list of its own |
| `{"enumSource": <its source>}` | the union of the values gathered beside it (§s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh) as literals | `Literal[<the values gathered beside it>]` | one of, with values from elsewhere |
| `{"oneOf": [<its members' schemas>]}` or `{"anyOf": [<its members' schemas>]}` | the union of the types that its members give | `Union[<the types that its members give>]` | — |
| `{"allOf": [<its members' schemas>]}` | the intersection of the types that its members give | a `TypedDict` of its own, which holds the fields of every member | — |
| `{"type": [<its types>]}` | the union of the types that the schema would give if each of its types in turn replaced the list | `Union[<those types>]` | — |
| `{"type": "null"}` | `null` | `None` | — |
| `{"type": "string"}` | `string` | `str` | text |
| `{"type": "string", "format": "email"}` | `string` | `str` | email address |
| `{"type": "string", "format": "date-time"}` | `string` | `str` | instant |
| `{"type": "string", "format": "date"}` | `string` | `str` | date |
| `{"type": "string", "format": "duration"}` | `string` | `str` | duration |
| `{"type": "integer"}`, with or without bounds | `number` | `int` | whole number |
| `{"type": "number"}`, with or without bounds | `number` | `float` | number |
| `{"type": "boolean"}` | `boolean` | `bool` | yes/no |
| `{"type": "array", "items": <its members' schema>}`, with or without bounds on how many members it holds | `<its members' type>[]` | `list[<its members' type>]` | list of |
| `{"properties": {<its fields>}}` | an object type written inline, its fields given as the fields of a RecordType are given (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b) | a `TypedDict` of its own | — |
| `{"type": "object", "additionalProperties": <its values' schema>}` | `Record<string, <its values' type>>` | `dict[str, <its values' type>]` | map of |
| `{}` | `unknown` | `Any` | any value |

A field's schema falls under the first row of the table whose keywords it holds with the values that the row gives. In a row, a value in angle brackets stands for any value of the kind that it names. Any other keyword of a field's schema, such as `description`, `format` or a bound, leaves the type as the row gives it. A schema that falls under no other row falls under the last, `{}`. The same table gives the type of the members of a list, of the values of a map and of the members of `oneOf`, `anyOf` and `allOf` from their schemas.

A field with `identifierOf` that fails the check of an identifier followed to its end (§s-3anv9qcmx8pwp2w) gives the same type as `{}`.

In Python, `Literal` can hold only a string, a whole number, `true`, `false` or `null`, so in Python a `const` with any other value, or an `enum` that holds any other value, gives the same type as `{}`. In `Literal`, `true`, `false` and `null` are written `True`, `False` and `None`.

An `allOf` gives a `TypedDict` of its own in Python only where each of its members gives a `TypedDict` in Python, and otherwise gives the same type as `{}`. That `TypedDict` holds the fields of the members, in the order of the members. A field that several members declare has the type that the last of them gives, as a field that a RecordType takes through `refines` does (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b). A field of that `TypedDict` is required where the `required` of at least one member of the `allOf` lists it.

In Python, each object written inline and each `allOf` that gives a `TypedDict` is written as a `TypedDict` of its own. Such a `TypedDict` is written only if a type uses it. It is written once, after every type that `sheriff types` writes for the RecordType whose `schema` holds it. It has the SpecTag (§s-5z5gnu7pahr82xp) of that RecordType. Its name begins with the name of that RecordType's type. One part follows for each step from that `schema` down to it, each with its first letter changed to uppercase:
- for a field, the field's name;
- for the members of a list, `Item`;
- for the values of a map, `Value`;
- for a member of `oneOf`, `anyOf` or `allOf`, its position in the list of members, counted from one.

For example, the object written inline as the field `address` of the RecordType `user` gives the `TypedDict` `UserAddress`. Such a name, too, cannot be generated in the cases that the node on what is generated from a RecordType lists (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b).

A RecordType's `schema` names another RecordType only in the following forms:
- a `$ref` whose value is `#` followed by the other RecordType's sid, which points to the `$anchor` of that RecordType's definition (§s-suv42g8r3ra2h6b);
- an `identifierOf` whose value is the other RecordType's sid.

`sheriff types` takes each value gathered beside a field (§s-ju5vcanbjph7mgh) once, in the type and in the RuntimeCheck (§s-e877bnfa559tvk9) in the same way, at the place where the value first appears in the field's `enumSource.gathered` (§s-5nf87c3e3jg9v7c).

In a file of RuntimeChecks, `sheriff types` writes each field's schema as the RecordType's `schema` holds it, with the following changes at any depth:
- `enumSource` is replaced by `enum`, which holds the values gathered beside the field;
- `identifierOf` is replaced, at the same position, by every keyword of the schema of the field at the end of the chain of identifiers, other than that schema's `description`;
- where the field fails the check of an identifier followed to its end (§s-3anv9qcmx8pwp2w), `identifierOf` is removed.
children.reason: JSON Schema is a standard with a validator in every language. Therefore, a field's schema serves as its RuntimeCheck, which checks in the same way in every language what a type in TypeScript or Python cannot express, such as a bound or a format. Each language's own type for a value is the one that its code reads without a conversion. An identifier has the type of the field that identifies the data records of the RecordType that it names. Therefore, a value that moves from that field to a field that refers to it keeps its type and passes the same RuntimeCheck.
examples: The `schema` of the RecordType `statement` holds `"accountId": {"identifierOf": "s-…", "description": "The account."}`, where `s-…` is the sid of the RecordType `account`. The field that identifies `account` is `number`, whose schema is `{"type": "string", "maxLength": 34}`. In TypeScript, `accountId` has the type `string`, and in the RuntimeChecks its schema is `{"type": "string", "maxLength": 34, "description": "The account."}`. The most likely mistake is to leave `identifierOf` in the RuntimeCheck: a JSON Schema validator does not recognise that keyword, so it does not check that `accountId` is a string.

decisions.problem: Nothing said what type an identifier of a data record has: text, as JSON:API requires of every identifier, or whatever the identified data record makes it from.
decisions.ruling: The owner: an identifier has the type of the field that identifies the data record it names, which that data record's node names, so that the type comes from the specification and the link from the identifier to that field can be checked.

decisions.problem: A field holding a day of the calendar had no neutral type but text, or an instant, which adds a time of day and an offset the day does not have; as text, two spellings of one day passed as two days, and a check of the spelling would have been written beside the data record. And the table gave no place to a bound on how many members a field of type list of holds.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a neutral type date is added, a day of the calendar with no time of day and no time zone, checked by the `date` format of JSON Schema; a field of type list of takes bounds on how many members it holds, named as JSON Schema names them.

decisions.problem: The values of a field of type `one of` were read from its own list and from the lists of domains, while the base now lets them come from the names of the domains and from the sids of a kind's nodes too. The order of several values coming from one node was not defined.
decisions.ruling: The owner: a field gives its own list's values, or those gathered beside it whatever their source, ordered by the node each comes from, the members of one list in their order.
